catalogTitle: מדליקין הנרות עד שאפילו הנפשות הנמוכות יאירו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah light, placed below ten tefachim and spreading outward night after night, is the Shechinah coming down to Jews in exile, and that each Jew, above all in his years of learning, must take in enough of its light to carry Torah into his whole life.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with ner ish u'veiso: beyond the miracle of the whole nation, each Jew should feel that a light burns for him personally. Yosef's two dreams show the same move, from Yosef watching from outside to the whole holy structure coming down to him in Egypt. The Chanukah light is placed below ten tefachim, although the Shechinah never descended below ten, because Chanukah is a festival of exile, a kind of bikur cholim in which Hashem comes down to the sick. Through the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel on the havdalah fire, the blue and white parts of a flame, and din and rachamim, he explains why the lights increase: one begins with aseh tov. He applies this to the years of yeshiva, criticizes young Jews who give themselves for foreign causes, reads the end of Niddah, and closes with Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who saw his whole life as a free gift and a miracle.

en: The mitzvah of ner ish u'veiso teaches that each Jew should feel the Chanukah miracle as something happening to him personally, not only to the nation.
The Chanukah light is placed below ten tefachim because Chanukah is a festival of exile, when the Shechinah comes down to the Jews as one visits the sick.
Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel reflect din and rachamim, the consuming blue and the illuminating white of a flame; the halachah follows Beis Hillel because the world now runs with rachamim.
The lights increase each night because, per Beis Hillel, one starts with aseh tov and the sur mera follows on its own.
The years of yeshiva are the time of chinuch, when a bochur must fill himself with enough Torah to light his way for the rest of his life.
Like Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, a Jew who knows that everything he has is a free gift sees his whole life as a chain of miracles.

title.en: A light that burns for each Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah light testifies to the miracles of the whole nation, but a distant person is barely moved by a national event. The mitzvah of ner ish u'veiso asks each Jew to feel that a light burns for him personally and that the same miracles happen in his own life.

title.en: Yosef's two dreams

summary.en: Chanukah falls in the weeks of Yosef's dreams. In the first dream Yosef only watches the sheaves from outside; in the second the sun, moon and stars bow to him, and the Mashgiach explains that the whole holy structure must come down to Yosef in exile in Egypt so that he does not sink there.

title.en: Below ten tefachim: the Shechinah visits the sick

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Chanukah light is placed below ten tefachim when the Shechinah never descended below ten, and answers that Chanukah is a festival of exile, when the Jews are sick, and at bikur cholim the great go down to the small, as with Chizkiyahu and Yeshayahu. He adds that the light of Chanukah must not only be received but lit onward to others.

title.en: Me'or or me'orei: the colors of a flame

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah where Beis Shammai say 'shebara me'or ha'esh' and Beis Hillel 'borei me'orei ha'esh', and describes the flame: a white part above that gives light, and a blue part around the wick that consumes the wick and the oil.

title.en: Din and rachamim in Shammai and Hillel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Beis Shammai follow midas hadin and Beis Hillel midas harachamim, both 'divrei Elokim chaim', and that the halachah follows Beis Hillel because the world now runs with rachamim. He brings the Ramban that positive mitzvos come from love and negative ones from fear, and links Beis Shammai to the consuming blue of the flame and Beis Hillel to its illuminating white.

title.en: Pochet or mosif: start with aseh tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the dispute over decreasing or increasing the lights to sur mera and aseh tov: Beis Shammai put the guarding from sin first, Beis Hillel the doing of good. He brings the offerings of Kayin and Hevel and the wool and linen of kilayim, and says a Jew must not hold back from avodas Hashem because of his sins; he should begin with aseh tov and the sur mera will follow.

title.en: Enough oil for the whole road

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah light must shine into the public domain, the exile where most of a Jew's life goes to parnassah. The years of chinuch in yeshiva are the time to pour in enough oil, enough Torah and yiras Shamayim, so that it burns 'until the foot leaves the market' and lights his whole way.

title.en: Guarding other people's vineyards

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'they made me a keeper of the vineyards, my own vineyard I did not keep' and laments talented Jewish young people who give themselves with mesiras nefesh for foreign causes and for peace, while Torah needs them. He says there will be no true peace until the days of Moshiach, and that the light of Torah must shine into the street.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the end of Niddah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the last days of Chanukah to the last period in yeshiva and asks whether one has prepared enough Torah. He reads the end of Masechta Niddah on halichos and halachos, and through a teaching of Rabbi Shalom of Belz on 'beiso zo ishto' explains that a Jew's life outside the beis medrash must be run by the Torah.

title.en: A Chanina in every generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Al Hanisim of Chanukah names Matisyahu's father Yochanan, and brings the Gemara that the whole world is fed for the sake of Chanina ben Dosa. He asks why the heavenly voice still says it generations later, and explains that in every generation there is a 'Chanina', a person who knows that all he has is a free gift and needs nothing for himself.

title.en: A life of miracles and the Chashmonaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why seeing 'Chanina' in a dream signals miracles: such a person sees even his bread and parnassah as a miracle, as Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa said that the One who told oil to burn can tell vinegar to burn. He explains that the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh came from knowing they had nothing, and closes with a brachah.

catalogTitle: צד א: חיזוק מחנוכה - יש לי חלק באלקי ישראל!

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah was born of the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and that every Jew gains his share in it, and proclaims that he has a part in the G-d of Israel, through small daily acts of giving up his own will.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah lights is especially dear, and explains that Chanukah alone among the festivals came about through mesiras nefesh, which is what makes it dear. A Jew's share in Chanukah follows his own mesiras nefesh. He defines nefesh as a person's will, so mesiras nefesh means giving up one's will: not looking at what one should not see, holding back a cutting remark. He tells his listeners to join the Chashmonaim and to answer the Greeks, who demanded that Jews write that they have no part in the G-d of Israel, by declaring on every mitzvah that they do have a part. He then links the month of Teves to the Me'aras haMachpelah and to Avraham Avinu, who set aside his own comfort but never another's, and ends with a call to help others, with the mashal of the fruit tree and the cedar.

en: The Rambam calls only the mitzvah of Chanukah lights especially dear, because Chanukah alone was established through mesiras nefesh.
A Jew's share in Chanukah is in proportion to his own mesiras nefesh for Torah and Yiddishkeit.
Nefesh means a person's will, so mesiras nefesh is any act in which a Jew gives up his own will for Hashem.
Against the Greeks' demand to write that Jews have no part in the G-d of Israel, a Jew should declare through every mitzvah that he has a part.
Avraham Avinu set aside his own comfort, sitting out for guests three days after his milah, but never imposed on the comfort of others.
Chanukah is a time to help others grow in Torah, like a tree that gives fruit, without fearing that one's own growth will suffer.

title.en: Why Chanukah is called especially dear

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Rambam calls only the mitzvah of Chanukah lights especially dear, and explains that Chanukah is the one festival brought about by the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh; what comes through mesiras nefesh is precious.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh means giving up one's will

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Chanukah is the time to remember the need for mesiras nefesh like the Chashmonaim, and that one's share in Chanukah follows it. He explains that nefesh means will, so mesiras nefesh is not only giving one's life but every act that goes against one's own will.

title.en: Torah as vessels; small acts of mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the words of Torah are vessels through which a Jew can grasp a holiness too great for creation to hold. He then gives everyday examples of mesiras nefesh: turning away from idle talk, not looking at what one should not see in the street, and holding back a sharp remark.

title.en: Joining the Chashmonaim: I have a part

summary.en: The Mashgiach says all of Chanukah exists because of the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and urges each Jew to join them. He brings the Greeks' demand that Jews write they have no part in the G-d of Israel, and says a Jew should declare on his mezuzah, tefillin, Chanukah lights and tzitzis that he does have a part.

title.en: Teves and the Me'aras haMachpelah

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the month of Teves to the Me'aras haMachpelah, which was not destroyed as Yerushalayim was, and says something of the Avos in every Jew can never be destroyed. He tells how Avraham discovered the cave and saw that all tefillos go up from there.

title.en: Avraham: one's own comfort, not another's

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person may set aside only his own comfort, never someone else's. Avraham Avinu would not inconvenience others, yet three days after his milah, in pain, he sat out to welcome guests.

title.en: Spreading holiness and helping others

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Greeks wanted to take over the territory of holiness, while Jews set the Chanukah light in the public domain and founded holiness there. He calls on his listeners to help others, such as a friend who does not understand the shiur, and brings the mashal of the fruit tree and the cedar; he closes by asking them to draw strength from the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh.

catalogTitle: The Greatness and Downfall of זמרי בן סלוא and how it Corresponds to חודש אב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach traces the three names of the Nasi of Shimon, Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Shaul ben haKenaanis and Zimri ben Salu, as his greatness, his fall and his coming tikkun, and shows how they correspond to the month of Av, the month of Shimon.

abstract.en: On the hilulah of the Arizal, the Mashgiach opens with the Arizal's teaching of gilgul: Hashem ensures that no neshama is ever lost. He turns to Parshas Pinchas, read as Av is blessed, and to Zimri ben Salu, who had three names. As Shaul ben haKenaanis he carried an impurity inherited from Dinah; as Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai he was the great Nasi of Shimon. The Arizal reveals that Zimri returned as Rabbi Akiva and Kozbi as the wife of Turnus Rufus. Since the months correspond to the tribes and Av is the month of Shimon, Av follows the same path: great, fallen, and destined to become a joyous Yom Tov. The Mashgiach then explains Rabbi Akiva's laughter at the fox on the Har HaBayis: the fox, shual, was Shaul ben haKenaanis, part of his own neshama coming to its tikkun. The ayin of galus will turn into an aleph, and the Mashgiach ends that now, close to the Geulah, is the time to lift up Av.

en: According to the Arizal's teaching of gilgul, Hashem brings every neshama back again and again until it reaches its perfection, so that no one is ever lost.
Zimri ben Salu had three names, Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Shaul ben haKenaanis and Zimri ben Salu, each marking a period of his greatness or his fall.
Zimri's fall came from an impurity inherited from Dinah, who was violated by Shechem; his essence remained pure.
The twelve months correspond to the twelve tribes, and Av, the fifth month, is the month of Shimon, whose Nasi was Zimri.
When Moshiach comes, Av will be a month of joy and Tisha B'Av will be like Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah.
Rabbi Akiva laughed at the fox in the Kodesh HaKodashim because he saw in it Shaul ben haKenaanis, a part of his own neshama coming to its tikkun.
The Mashgiach says the Geulah seems very close, and now is the time to work hard to lift Av from the ground to where it belongs.

title.en: The Arizal and the secret of gilgul

summary.en: On the hilulah of the Arizal, the Mashgiach compares the Torah to a garden with gems hidden below its surface, and explains that one pillar of the Arizal's teaching is gilgul: Hashem devises ways so that no neshama is ever lost.

title.en: Shaul ben haKenaanis: the source of Zimri's fall

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Zimri ben Salu and his three names, and explains the name Shaul ben haKenaanis: Zimri lent himself to sin because of an impurity inherited from Dinah, though his essence was pure.

title.en: Shelumiel's lost name and the Arizal's gilgulim

summary.en: As Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai he was the great Nasi of Shimon; when he fell, Pinchas took the name of Shakai and became Eliyahu, the angel of the bris. The Mashgiach then brings the Arizal that Zimri returned as Rabbi Akiva and Kozbi as the wife of Turnus Rufus, and links the 24,000 who died to Rabbi Akiva's 24,000 students.

title.en: Av is the month of Shimon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the twelve months correspond to the twelve tribes in the order of the Nesiim's offerings, so Av is the month of Shimon, whose Nasi bore all three names, and he describes Av as a sorrowful month.

title.en: The future greatness of Av

summary.en: Rather than the mourning of Av, the Mashgiach speaks of its greatness: Zechariah's promise that the fasts will become days of joy, and the sefarim's comparison of the three weeks to the days from Rosh Hashanah to Simchas Torah. He describes Zimri's original greatness as Nasi, whose day in Nisan is still a Yom Tov, ties Shimon to Nisan, and brings the Medrash that Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva laughs at the fox

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Gemara at the end of Makkos: the Tannaim wept at a fox leaving the Kodesh HaKodashim while Rabbi Akiva laughed, since the fulfilled prophecy of destruction assures the prophecy of comfort. He notes the Rambam's view that the place keeps its holiness, and asks why the Gemara stresses the wording of their reply.

title.en: Everything has its place; Rabbi Akiva's two laughs

summary.en: Bringing the Maharal that everything has its place according to its neshama, the Mashgiach asks what the fox was doing in the Kodesh HaKodashim. He compares Rabbi Akiva's laughter at the wife of Turnus Rufus, whom he foresaw would convert and become his wife, and concludes that the fox too was part of Rabbi Akiva's neshama: shual is Shaul ben haKenaanis.

title.en: The fox, the vineyard and Akiva nichamtanu

summary.en: The fox stands for the zenus that destroys the vineyard of Jewish purity, the sin of Zimri; seeing it in the Kodesh HaKodashim, the place of atonement, Rabbi Akiva saw Zimri's tikkun beginning. The Mashgiach adds that shual is the gematria of Zimri ben Salu and 'Akiva nichamtanu' the gematria of Kozbi bas Tzur.

title.en: From ayin to aleph

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that an ayin turning into an aleph marks a tikkun: the suspended ayin of 'chazir miyaar', and Rabbi Meir's 'kasnos or' with an aleph. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that galus always carries the ayin of seventy, and that Shaul only lent himself to sin and did not sell his neshama.

title.en: Shimon will rise: the future of Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up: Shimon was great, fell, began to rise through Rabbi Akiva, and will fully rise when Tisha B'Av becomes a Yom Tov. Adam's garment of skin will become a garment of light, the gematria of Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai, and he ends that the Geulah seems close and now is the time to work hard to lift up Av.

catalogTitle: צד ב: מגודל אהבת הקב"ה אלינו הוא נותן לנו עוד זמן לשוב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that out of His love Hashem extends the time for teshuvah past Yom Kippur until the last day of Chanukah, and that Chanukah calls on every Jew to renew himself through Torah and tefillah against the foreign culture entering his home.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the extensions of the time for teshuvah: the Gemara says tzaddikim are sealed on Rosh Hashanah while beinonim wait until Yom Kippur, the judgment is handed over only on Shemini Atzeres, and the chassidishe seforim bring from the Arizal that the time lasts until Zos Chanukah, an extension given for later, smaller generations. He counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah, 122, and shows the periods hinted in the number of pesukim of the parshiyos read then, with Ki Savo's 122 pesukim matching the full extension. Ki Savo belongs to the ending year, so it asks what was done with last year's 122 days, and he points to the hard events of the past year. Turning to Chanukah, he describes the Jews' mesirus nefesh against Greek ways, warns that today radio, newspapers, television and the internet bring the outside world into the home, and calls for kindling the lights of Torah. Through the reading of the nesiim, the Targum Yonasan and the Gemara in Sanhedrin he teaches that the real war is fought with Torah, tefillah and chessed, and ends with a call to use the extension to become a better Jew.

en: The time for teshuvah is extended in stages: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Shemini Atzeres when the judgment is sent out, and Zos Chanukah, as the chassidishe seforim bring from the Arizal.
From Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah there are 122 days, and the stages of teshuvah are hinted in the number of pesukim of the parshiyos read in that season.
The extension until Chanukah was given because later, smaller generations could not finish their teshuvah by Yom Kippur as the great generations did.
Today the outside world, through radio, newspapers, television and the internet, has entered the Jewish home, and Chanukah calls for kindling the lights of Torah against it.
The war of the Jewish people is fought in every beis medrash, with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, as the Chashmonaim fought.

title.en: Extensions of the time for teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists how Hashem keeps extending the time for teshuvah: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Shemini Atzeres, and, as the seforim bring from the Arizal, Zos Chanukah. He explains the last extension was given for later, smaller generations.

title.en: Counting 122 days and the hint in the parshiyos

summary.en: The Mashgiach counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah and arrives at 122. He shows that the stages of teshuvah are hinted in the number of pesukim of the parshiyos read in this season, such as Haazinu's 52.

title.en: Ki Savo's 122 pesukim and the past year

summary.en: Someone pointed out to the Mashgiach that Parshas Ki Savo has 122 pesukim. He asks why the hint is in the parsha of the tochachah and explains that it belongs to the ending year, asking what was done with last year's 122 days, and he recalls the painful events of the past year before calling for a fresh start.

title.en: Chanukah against the foreign culture at home

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the mesirus nefesh of the Jews against the Greeks for Torah and Yiddishkeit, warns against a Jew who learns and davens but whose outlook is goyish, and says that today radio, newspapers, television and the internet have turned the private home into a public domain. He ends with a call to kindle the lights of Torah.

title.en: The nesiim and the time of renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the parsha of the nesiim is read on Chanukah: the Mishkan was finished in Kislev but dedicated in Nissan, and Kislev received the Chanukah of the Chashmonaim. Chanukah is a time of chinuch and renewal like Rosh Hashanah, and he brings the Targum Yonasan that the nesiim read on Chanukah stand against the twelve princes of Yishmael.

title.en: The real war is in the beis medrash

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the war of Yishmael against Klal Yisroel is not decided by weapons in Eretz Yisroel or Afghanistan but in every beis medrash, through Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, as the Chashmonaim fought. He brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin on being saved from chevlei Moshiach and closes with a call to use the extension until Zos Chanukah to become a better Jew, with a brachah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: אור המשיח נתגלה ע”י מסירת נפש (שייכות לפרשת וישב)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the light of Moshiach hidden in Chanukah and in Parshas Vayeshev is revealed only through mesirus nefesh, and that this is the bond between Vayeshev, Chanukah and Yud-Tes Kislev.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Maggid's demand that a ba'al korei know how each parsha connects to its week, and asks how Vayeshev connects to Yud-Tes Kislev. Chanukah, he explains, is the revelation of the hidden light of Moshiach: its mitzvah goes below ten tefachim into the public domain, to kindle souls that have fallen under the sitra achra. This is why the one Mishnah touching Chanukah speaks of a lamp placed below ten tefachim, and why Chanukah was little discussed until generations close to Moshiach. In Vayeshev the souls of both Moshiachs are hidden: Yehudah goes down, and Tamar waits until she is already burning before sending to him, because the Satan cannot stand against mesirus nefesh. Yosef, too, shows mesirus nefesh with Potiphar's wife, as did the Chashmonaim. The Mashgiach closes with the mesirus nefesh of the Alter Rebbe, the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rayatz, and says a Jew today must have mesirus nefesh.

en: Chanukah is the revelation of the hidden light, the light of Moshiach, which every Jew carries within him in a concealed way.
Unlike the Shechinah, which never descended below ten tefachim, the Chanukah light goes below ten tefachim into the public domain to reach souls that have fallen under the sitra achra.
The souls of Moshiach ben Dovid and Moshiach ben Yosef are hidden in Parshas Vayeshev, in the descent of Yehudah and the birth of Peretz, and in Yosef's descent to Egypt.
The Satan cannot accuse against mesirus nefesh, so whoever brings Moshiach must have mesirus nefesh, as Tamar, Yehudah and Yosef did.
The Chanukah miracle itself came through the mesirus nefesh of the Chashmonaim, and a Jew who lights the Chanukah candle draws in the light of Moshiach.
The Chabad leaders, from the Alter Rebbe on, spread pnimiyus haTorah with mesirus nefesh, and this links Yud-Tes Kislev to Vayeshev and Chanukah.

title.en: The Maggid's ba'al korei and the question of Vayeshev

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Maggid of Mezritch asked the young Shneur Zalman whether he knew the connection of each parsha to its week before making him his ba'al korei, and asks what connects Parshas Vayeshev to Yud-Tes Kislev. He begins with the seforim's teaching that Chanukah reveals the light of Moshiach.

title.en: Chanukah goes below ten tefachim

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Gemara that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim with the Chanukah light, which is placed below ten tefachim in the public domain to kindle fallen souls with the hidden light. He then notes that the Mishnah and the early generations say almost nothing about Chanukah, unlike Purim, while the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Bnei Yissaschar speak of it at length.

title.en: Why Chanukah was hidden, and the one Mishnah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the hidden light of Chanukah stayed concealed in earlier generations, which were not yet close to Moshiach; Chanukah reaches even the 'refuse oils' that Shabbos cannot light, the souls Moshiach will gather from the ends of the heavens. He then explains why the Mishnah's only Chanukah law is the camel and the lamp below ten tefachim: that law holds the whole essence of Chanukah.

title.en: Moshiach's soul hidden in Vayeshev

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the souls of both Moshiachs are hidden in Vayeshev: Yehudah goes down, and Peretz is born from Tamar in a concealed way so that there should be no accusation, illustrated with a parable of a man who hid his money in the thief's own sack. He then asks why Tamar waited until she was taken out to be burned before sending her proof to Yehudah.

title.en: Tamar's mesirus nefesh defeats the Satan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the fire had already caught Tamar's garments when she sent to Yehudah, who admitted at once. He explains that the Satan had blocked Moshiach through Er and Onan, who later came back as Peretz and Zerach, so Tamar used the one thing the Satan cannot oppose, mesirus nefesh, and Yehudah accepted the shame with mesirus nefesh as well.

title.en: Yosef and the Chashmonaim: Moshiach through mesirus nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same mesirus nefesh in Yosef, ancestor of Moshiach ben Yosef, who withstood Potiphar's wife's threats and fled without his garment. Both Moshiachs had to descend; the Chashmonaim likewise fought the mighty Greek kingdom with mesirus nefesh, and so Chanukah is the light of Moshiach that a Jew draws in when he lights the Chanukah candle.

title.en: The Alter Rebbe and the Tzemach Tzedek

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the first Chassidic sefer, Toldos Yaakov Yosef, began the revelation of the Torah of Moshiach, pnimiyus haTorah, which aroused an accusation in heaven, and that the Alter Rebbe's deeper spreading of it led to his arrest in Russia, where he declared himself a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov and was accused of sending money to Eretz Yisroel. He then tells how the Tzemach Tzedek refused to sign a blank letter in Moscow and was let go.

title.en: The Rayatz, the shluchim, and mesirus nefesh today

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Rayatz's mesirus nefesh in spreading Torah under the Communists and his demand that his chassidim do the same, and ties together Chanukah, Kislev, Vayeshev and Yud-Tes Kislev as days of mesirus nefesh. He mentions shluchim going to desolate places to kindle extinguished souls with the power of pnimiyus haTorah, says a Jew today must have mesirus nefesh, and closes with a brachah for the light of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: א: מסירת נפש על “ישראל גוי אחד בארץ”

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the name Yisrael, the oneness of 'goy echad', was earned through the mesiras nefesh of the sons of Yaakov at Shechem, the same mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim that Chanukah and its lamp at the door stand for.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the 613 mitzvos and seven rabbinic mitzvos corresponding to the 620 letters of the Aseres Hadibros, and the 600,000 letters of the Torah corresponding to the souls of Israel. Ner Chanukah, the last mitzvah, corresponds to the lowest Jew of the generation before Moshiach. He describes the mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim and of Chabad in Soviet Russia. He then asks why Yaakov received the name Yisrael only after Shechem, and brings the Divrei Yoel on why the people of Shechem accepted milah: to prevent a separate Jewish nation. The war of Shechem parallels the war of Chanukah; Chanukah's twenty-fifth day corresponds to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael, the acceptance of mesiras nefesh. After a story of Reb Naftali of Ropshitz, he explains Yaakov's setting of techumim and the Chanukah lamp at the door as a boundary between Israel and the nations, and closes with Chabad's shluchim.

en: Ner Chanukah, the last of the seven rabbinic mitzvos, corresponds to the lowest Jew, the souls of the generation before Moshiach.
The Chashmonaim went out to war with mesiras nefesh and no natural chance of success, trusting in the eternity of Israel and of the Torah.
The people of Shechem accepted milah because the wicked cannot bear a separate Jewish nation bound to Hashem, and wanted to assimilate it away.
The name Yisrael expresses the oneness of Israel with Hashem, and it was earned only through the mesiras nefesh of Shechem.
Chanukah, on its twenty-fifth day, is the yom tov of Shema Yisrael, which means accepting mesiras nefesh.
The Chanukah lamp placed at the doorway is a boundary between the domain of Israel and the public domain of the nations.

He then describes the mesiras nefesh of the Chashmonaim and of Chabad in Soviet Russia.

title.en: Why the name Yisrael came after Shechem

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem waited until after Shechem to name Yaakov Yisrael, explains that the name expresses Israel's oneness with Hashem, and brings the Divrei Yoel on why the people of Shechem accepted milah: to prevent the rise of a separate Jewish nation.

title.en: Shechem, Chanukah and Shema Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws the parallel between the war of the sons of Yaakov at Shechem and the war of the Chashmonaim against the Greeks, both for the holiness of the Jewish family, and explains that the twenty-fifth of Kislev corresponds to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael, the acceptance of mesiras nefesh.

title.en: Tzaddikim speak to Hashem: Reb Naftali's milk

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when tzaddikim speak to people they are speaking to Hashem, and tells how Reb Naftali of Ropshitz demanded strong milk in his kitchen just before a nursing mother came for help. He applies this to the sons of Yaakov, whose words to Shechem were a plea to Hashem for a wall between Israel and the nations.

title.en: Techum Shabbos and the lamp at the door

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov's first act at Shechem was to set techumim: Shabbos is the private domain of oneness with Hashem, and assimilation is like carrying out into the public domain. The difference between Israel and the nations is like that between Shabbos and the weekdays, and the Chanukah lamp at the door marks that boundary.

title.en: The name Yisrael earned; Chabad's shluchim

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the name Yisrael was earned through the mesiras nefesh of Shechem, not at the meeting with the angel. He calls the Rebbes and chassidim of Chabad Yochanan Kohen Gadol and his soldiers, who keep sending shluchim even after shluchim were killed, and closes with a blessing.

catalogTitle: דרוש נפלא על טעמי המקרא - Golus is Rooted in Geulah - (ט' באב שחל בשבת)

oneLiner.en: Through the rare cantillation notes on 'alpayim ba'amah', the Mashgiach shows that the churban of Av is rooted in the geulah of Nissan, and that the scattering of galus and the forgotten neshamos of the gid hanasheh are meant to be gathered back.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the calendar's cycle of rising and falling, in which Tammuz and Av belong to Esav. He then asks why the rare cantillation notes karnei parah and yerach ben yomo appear only on 'alpayim ba'amah' in Parshas Masei. Building on the Midrash that the first day of Pesach fixes the day of Tisha B'Av, he shows that churban is rooted in geulah. Av draws from Nissan as Shimon drew from Yehuda; karnei parah, the segmented cow's horn, stands for Av's division, and yerach ben yomo for Nissan, whose every day is as fresh as Rosh Chodesh. The shofar, symbol of ingathering, unites the two. He then explains Yaakov's gift to Esav, the gid hanasheh and Dina's daughter Osnas as lost neshamos that will return, and closes with the strength of Shabbos when Tisha B'Av falls on it.

en: Because the first day of Pesach determines the day of the week of Tisha B'Av, the Mashgiach concludes that the churban is rooted in the geulah and exists for its sake.
The month of Av, the month of Shimon, receives its blessing from Nissan, the month of Yehuda, just as Shimon received his portion in Eretz Yisrael from within Yehuda's.

Karnei parah, named for the segmented horn of a cow, represents the division of Av, while yerach ben yomo represents Nissan, whose every day stays as fresh as Rosh Chodesh; the second serves the first and prepares it for the birth of Moshiach.
The scattering of galus, hinted in the note pazer, has the inner purpose of gathering the lost sparks and neshamos from among the nations.
The gid hanasheh that Yaakov lost to Esav's angel stands for forgotten Jewish neshamos under Esav's rule, and Tisha B'Av is the day that corresponds to it.
When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, Shabbos pushes it away and hints at the time when the gid hanasheh will be healed and the lost neshamos will return to Yaakov.

title.en: The calendar's descent and two rare notes

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the rise and fall of the calendar year, with Tammuz and Av belonging to Esav and the slide down after Sivan. He then notes that the words 'alpayim ba'amah' in Parshas Masei carry two notes found nowhere else in the Torah, karnei parah and yerach ben yomo, and asks why.

title.en: Pesach fixes Tisha B'Av: churban rooted in geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on Eichah that the first day of Pesach and Tisha B'Av fall on the same weekday, by the order of at-bash, and the Pri Tzaddik that a Pesach on Shabbos is a sign of a good year. He concludes that the churban is rooted in the geulah, as Yocheved was born on the way into Mitzrayim and Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Av receives from Nissan; the lion and the lamb

summary.en: Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the Mashgiach matches the months to the tribes: Av is Shimon's month and Nissan is Yehuda's, and as Shimon's portion and blessing came through Yehuda, Av draws from Nissan. He adds that the mazal of Av, the lion, is rooted in chesed and in the mazal of Nissan, the lamb.

title.en: The seven pazers: scattering to gather

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the great Shabbosos of the three weeks and of the seven pazer notes in Parshas Beha'aloscha, read as the year slides down. Pazer means scattering, galus among the nations, but with its milui it equals kibbutz galuyos: the scattering is meant to gather the sparks and lost Jews, and it is answered by the seven haftaros of consolation.

title.en: Why a cow's horn is no shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that every shofar is valid except a cow's, and Abaye's reason that a cow's horn grows in segments and looks like several shofros. He explains that the shofar symbolizes the gathering of all Jews, while the cow's horn is division, like pazer, and so it hints at Av, whose churban came through baseless hatred.

title.en: Masei, the Shelah on Nissan, and 'ben yomo'

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the first letters of 'Eleh masei bnei Yisrael' hint at the four exiles. He brings the Shelah that every day of Nissan is Rosh Chodesh, and explains the halachic term ben yomo, a vessel that absorbed within the day and is still fresh, calling Nissan a month that never goes stale.

title.en: Yerach ben yomo serves karnei parah

summary.en: The Mashgiach identifies yerach ben yomo with Nissan and karnei parah with Av, and explains that Nissan serves Av, bringing unity into the month of division and preparing it for the birth of Moshiach. The shofar with its milui equals both notes together, and karnei parah equals David Melech Yisrael; this is read on the first Shabbos of Av to strengthen Jews weary of galus.

title.en: The migrash, fresh love, and the vessels of Midian

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a migrash of two thousand amos is the outskirts where one is driven out, yet it stays within the techum of the city, and that Nissan shows Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael never going stale. He then asks why the Torah required kashering Midian's vessels even when not ben yomo, and answers that Bilam tried to make that love lose its freshness, so Midian's forbidden taste never goes stale.

title.en: Esav's share in time and Yaakov's gift

summary.en: After a short interruption, the Mashgiach explains that the journeys exist in time as well as place: the three weeks belong to Esav, and Tisha B'Av is Esav's portion, a day of mourning. He brings Yaakov's gift to Esav and the Midrash that Yaakov's flocks were Jewish neshamos, so the animals that went to Esav stand for neshamos that stray into Esav's domain.

title.en: The gid hanasheh: forgotten neshamos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the wrestle with Esav's angel Yaakov won but was injured in the thigh, which the seforim read as descendants lost to Esav. Nasheh means forgetting, so the gid hanasheh is the forgotten neshamos, of whom Tziyon says 'Hashem has forgotten me', and he gives a gematria linking those words to Menachem Av.

title.en: Dina, Shechem and Osnas

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that what happened symbolically with the angel happened in fact in Shechem: Dina was taken, yet Yaakov lost nothing. Dina's daughter Osnas, hidden in a thornbush and brought to Mitzrayim, became Yosef's wife and the mother of Moshiach ben Yosef, so a hidden spark of Moshiach was in Shechem.

title.en: Seven consolations; Tisha B'Av as the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven haftaros of consolation answer the seven pazers and assure Knesses Yisrael it will not be forgotten, since the scattering was meant to add converts and gather the lost. He brings the Zohar that the 365 days match the 365 sinews and Tisha B'Av is the gid hanasheh, and a Midrash reading 'minchah yashivu' as the return of Yaakov's gift to Esav.

title.en: Shechem's hidden spark and Dina's destiny

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the Shechem episode had the purpose of pazer, to be scattered in order to bring back, and that Shechem ben Chamor equals in gematria 'haMelech haMashiach ben Yosef'. Dina was meant to be Yosef and was switched, so she was destined from birth to provide Yosef's match. Tisha B'Av, lost to Esav, will return as a festival, as Zechariah says.

title.en: Shabbos Tisha B'Av heals the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Shabbos zemiros about Edom end with a passuk of geulah, and explains that eating on Tisha B'Av is like eating the gid hanasheh. When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos it hints at the time the gid hanasheh will be healed; so too Yaakov arrived 'shalem', healed, in Shechem, on Shabbos.

title.en: We are the lost neshamos; the strength of Shabbos Chazon

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that all of us, even those who keep Shabbos, are lost neshamos compared with earlier generations, and that these weeks are a time to return to Yaakov's flocks with bitachon and emunah. He closes with the moon on Tisha B'Av, the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash on Shabbos Chazon, and the Shabbos that pushes away Esav's angel, ending with the passuk of the consolation of Tziyon.

catalogTitle: ב: אלקי אבטח בך

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that true bitachon means doing what Hashem wants without fear of loss or mockery, and shows that the Chashmonaim's victory, and the mitzvah of Chanukah itself, rest on this trust.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach defines bitachon as doing the right thing with certainty that Hashem will not let one lose by it, and says anger is a sign of lacking emunah and bitachon, since no one can do good or harm without Hashem's will, as Dovid HaMelech showed when Shimi ben Gera cursed him. A Midrash about a man saved because he relied on being the king's relative explains 'Elokai becha batachti'. The test of bitachon is not fearing mockery: Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah were saved in the merit of Yaakov, whom the wicked mocked, and the Shulchan Aruch opens with not being ashamed before scoffers. The thirteen Chashmonaim, hopelessly outnumbered, went to war with bitachon and said 'Yoshev b'seser'. Chanukah, the last rabbinic mitzvah, belongs to the last generation, and its mitzvah, 'ner ish uveiso', is a mitzvah of the family, which leads to an appeal for hachnasas kallah.

en: Bitachon means doing what is right with certainty that Hashem will not let one lose by it; one who expects to regret it later has no bitachon.
Anger is a sign that a person lacks emunah and bitachon, since no one can do good or harm without Hashem's will.
The test of bitachon is not being impressed by mockery when doing Hashem's will, which is why the Shulchan Aruch opens with not being ashamed before scoffers.
The Chashmonaim, outnumbered in every way, went to war with bitachon that Hashem would not let the Torah be uprooted, and said 'Yoshev b'seser', a psalm of pure bitachon.
Chanukah is the last mitzvah the Rabbanan instituted, and belongs to the last souls of the generation before Moshiach, who should strengthen themselves even when they see little merit in themselves.
The mitzvah of Chanukah, 'ner ish uveiso', is placed on the family rather than on the individual, and like a family it grows from day to day.

title.en: Bitachon, anger and the king's relative

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines bitachon as acting with certainty that Hashem will not let one lose, calls anger a sign of missing emunah, and brings Dovid HaMelech's response to Shimi ben Gera. He then tells the Midrash's parable of a man spared because he relied on being the king's relative, explaining 'Elokai becha batachti'.

title.en: The test of bitachon: not fearing mockery

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the true test of bitachon knowing that Hashem wants one's service despite trials and ridicule, and brings the Midrash on Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who were saved from the fire in the merit of Yaakov, whom the wicked mocked.

title.en: The Chashmonaim went to war with bitachon

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Shulchan Aruch opens with not being ashamed before scoffers, then describes the thirteen Chashmonaim, outnumbered in every way, going to war trusting that Hashem would not let the Torah be uprooted. They said 'Yoshev b'seser', a psalm of bitachon that mentions no merit, and this, he says, is the idea of Chanukah.

title.en: The last mitzvah and the mitzvah of the family

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah, the last rabbinic mitzvah, belongs to the last generation, and that 'ner ish uveiso' makes it a mitzvah of the family that grows each day. He closes by linking this to the gathering for hachnasas kallah and wishes a joyous Chanukah.

catalogTitle: “ה' אלקי יגיה חשכי” - האור הגנוז מאיר בתוך החושך

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah light is the hidden light (or haganuz) that Hashem sends down into the deepest darkness, as it came down to Yosef in Egypt, and that Zos Chanukah, which includes the whole of Chanukah, is a day of emunah and of thanking Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the difference between the private domain, the domain of Hashem, and the public domain: Chanukah is lit at the door, where the Jew goes out into the long night of exile, and there Hashem sends the hidden light. He applies this to the descent into Egypt: Yocheved, Serach and above all Yosef, whom no one recognized because he was the hidden light. On the day of Yosef's test, the idolaters' festival, he could not be saved by Torah, so the Kisei HaKavod came down to him; the Mashgiach suggests that day was Chanukah, near the tekufah. Yosef is a sign for his children that in the worst darkness Hashem holds a Jew's hand: 'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki'. Zos Chanukah, the final sealing after Rosh Hashanah, includes all the lights and is for those who live by emunah alone. He ends with thanking Hashem, coming on time to davening, and a brachah.

en: The Chanukah light is lit at the door because it belongs to the place where a Jew goes out from Hashem's private domain into the public domain of darkness, and there Hashem sends down the hidden light.
A Jew who finds himself in darkness should take Chanukah along and know that the hidden light is concealed in that darkness; when he believes it, it is revealed.
Yosef was the hidden light, which is why no one recognized him, and in his double darkness in Egypt the Kisei HaKavod came down to him.
Yosef is a sign for his children: even when a Jew cannot hold on to a word of davening or learning, Hashem holds his hand in the middle of the darkness.
Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, includes the whole of Chanukah and is the final sealing for those who were not sealed on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Chanukah is a time of thanks: the Mashgiach says a Jew should fix in himself the belief that Hashem does far more for him than he deserves, and take on to thank Him for every small thing.

title.en: Chanukah at the door of the public domain

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every matter is tied to its time, and contrasts the private domain, Hashem's domain, with the public domain. The Chanukah light belongs at the door where Klal Yisrael goes out into the long night of exile, and there Hashem sends the hidden light, as in 'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki'.

title.en: Taking Chanukah into the darkness; Yosef unrecognized

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew who finds himself in darkness should remember that the hidden light is concealed there. The descent to Egypt needed such a light: Yocheved, born at the entrance, and Serach, who brought Yaakov the good news; and Yosef, who was the hidden light and therefore was not recognized.

title.en: Yosef's double darkness and the Kisei HaKavod

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on the day of Yosef's test he was in a place of darkness and a time of darkness, the idolaters' festival, and could not protect himself through Torah; so the Kisei HaKavod came down to him. Yosef became the vessel for the hidden light, and the Mashgiach ties the thirty-six Chanukah lights to the thirty-six tzaddikim, with Yosef at their head.

title.en: Yosef's test fell on Chanukah

summary.en: After saying that some matters are better not thought about, the Mashgiach explains that on Chanukah one goes out into the public domain, and that whatever exists in holiness has its opposite. He suggests that the day of Yosef's test, near the winter tekufah, was Chanukah, and connects the twenty-fifth day with the twenty-fifth letter missing from 'Baruch Shem'.

title.en: Yosef as a sign: Hashem holds the hand in the dark

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef, left without Torah to save him, became a sign for his children: when Jews in the worst times cannot hold on to a word of davening or learning, Hashem still holds their hand. He brings the Midrash that darkness is Greece and explains 'Hashem Elokai yagiah choshki' with a parable of a commentary written on a hard sefer; then he ties 'kehayom hazeh' to the twenty-fifth of Kislev.

title.en: Zos Chanukah: the final sealing that includes all

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the seforim and the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah is the final sealing of Rosh Hashanah, and contrasts the light of the eighth day with the darkness of the nations' new year. The eight nights correspond to the attributes of mercy that are 'mazal', above merit, for those who live by emunah; the eighth day is like the Holy of Holies and includes all, as all the Nesi'im are read.

title.en: Burning the wicks; Chanukah as thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the custom of burning all the leftover wicks and oil on Zos Chanukah, showing that the day includes the whole Chanukah. He says its avodah is a bit of emunah that every Jew is a tzaddik, and that Chanukah is for thanks: one can never thank Hashem enough, and the eight days teach a Jew to thank Him for every small thing.

title.en: Coming on time to davening; closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks people to come on time to davening and say Hodu with the minyan, mentions Jews who need yeshuos and a segulah of saying Ketores with the tzibbur, and adds his own segulah of saying Hodu together with the minyan. He ends with taking on to thank Hashem, the bond of davening and learning, and a brachah that the darkness flee and the light of the eighth candle shine.

catalogTitle: צד א: יום של אמונה בדברים שהם למעלה מהשגתינו.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah, and above all Zos Chanukah, comes from a realm above human understanding, so its light and its good sealing for the Jewish people rest on their simple emunah in what they cannot grasp.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's question 'Mai Chanukah', asked of no other Yom Tov, and explains that the answer, eight days, is itself the point: eight is above the seven days of nature, and Chanukah comes from a world one may ask about but cannot know. He finds this in the name Chashmonaim, made of shemen, the letter ches and 'mai', and in oil, which always rises. With a mashal of a king who jumps into the mud for his child, he explains why this light still descends below ten handbreadths, the one Chanukah law hinted in the Mishnah. The miracle broke the Greek demand to understand everything. Through the Ramban, the Chiddushei HaRim and the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that the hidden light of Chanukah never goes out, like Shemini Atzeres. Zos Chanukah completes the Rosh Hashanah judgment, and Hashem then finds hidden merits in every Jew, as the Imrei Emes teaches from Parshas Mikeitz.

en: Chanukah lasts eight days, and eight stands above the seven days of nature, so Chanukah comes from a realm one cannot understand.
Greek wisdom held that one believes only what one understands, and the Chanukah miracle broke that impurity through simple emunah.
The light of Chanukah is the hidden light that is never extinguished, and in it lies the eternity of the Jewish people.
The judgment that begins on Rosh Hashanah comes from the hidden world and is completed on Zos Chanukah.
Jews merit a good sealing on Zos Chanukah because they believe in Hashem and in things they cannot understand.
On Zos Chanukah Hashem finds hidden merits in every Jew, merits even the greatest angels could not find.

title.en: Why the Gemara asks 'Mai Chanukah'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara asks 'what is Chanukah' about no other Yom Tov, and explains that its answer, eight days, shows Chanukah comes from a realm above nature that one may ask about but cannot know. This is why Jews are sealed for good on Zos Chanukah without a reason one can explain.

title.en: Chashmonaim, oil, and the king's child

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the name Chashmonaim as shemen, ches and 'mai', and explains that oil always rises above, belonging to the realm of eight. With a mashal of a king who jumps into the mud to save his child, he explains why the Shechinah nevertheless descends below ten handbreadths on Chanukah.

title.en: The one Chanukah law in the Mishnah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Mishnah contains no Chanukah laws except one deduced from it, that the Chanukah light belongs below ten handbreadths, and connects this to Rebbi, of the house of Dovid and the aspect of Moshiach. He then explains that Greek wisdom demanded understanding everything, and the miracle from the realm above reason broke that impurity.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the eternal menorah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the eighth day is the answer to 'Mai Chanukah', and in it lies Hashem's love for the Jewish people and the secret of their eternity. He brings Rashi and the Ramban on Beha'alosecha, that Aharon was told his share is forever, and the Chiddushei HaRim, that Aharon's menorah was hidden still burning.

title.en: The eighth is never nullified

summary.en: Bringing the Bnei Yissaschar that the Chanukah lights shine with the hidden light, the Mashgiach compares Chanukah to Shemini Atzeres, whose blessing stays because the eighth is above this world. He then connects Chanukah to Rosh Hashanah through the verse 'beyond the river your fathers dwelt from olam', reading olam as the hidden world.

title.en: 'Lo chen haresha'im': belief in the hidden

summary.en: From 'kein asah es hamenorah' and the Midrash on 'lo chen haresha'im', the Mashgiach explains that the wicked, followers of Greek wisdom, deny what they cannot see, while Jews believe in Hashem, the Torah and the Chanukah miracle. For that emunah alone they are sealed for good, and the wicked have no standing in that judgment.

title.en: Hashem finds merits: the Imrei Emes on Mikeitz

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Imrei Emes on 'HaElokim matza es avon avadecha': the shevatim were so pure that even their fault had to be searched for and 'found'. Through Rashi's kal vachomer in that parshah he explains that if this is so for judgment, how much more Hashem searches out and finds hidden merits in every Jew in the week of Chanukah.

title.en: The hidden light in every Jew; rejoicing and thanks

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that on Zos Chanukah the hidden light in every Jew comes out and by its light his merit is written for good. He calls for joy in Zos Chanukah and in emunah, and asks everyone to come on time to daven the next morning and say Hallel together, thanking Hashem for all the mitzvos and minhagim of Chanukah.

title.en: Blessing: the seal of the Kohen Gadol

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the gathering with a good sealing, describing Hashem as the Kohen Gadol whose seal the Greeks could not touch, and every Jew sealed on Zos Chanukah with the seal of oil. The shiur ends with singing.

catalogTitle: A Deeper Understanding of נחלת בני ראובן ובני גד and the Hidden Kedushah of the Three Weeks

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad sensed that the land east of the Jordan holds the hidden, higher kedushah of the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, which corresponds to the Three Weeks, whose concealed holiness will be revealed when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke of Bnei Gad and Bnei Reuven and asks why he says 'I know you have much livestock' and why the Torah stresses 'atzum me'od'. Following the Midrash and Sfas Emes, their portion was truly theirs, but they hurried to take it. He then builds a structure: of the ten maamaros the first three are beyond grasp, and of the ten nations promised to Avraham the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni (Ammon, Moav, Esav) are hidden under a great tumah that covers a greater kedushah. These correspond to the Three Weeks before the seven weeks of consolation. Reuven the firstborn and Gad, the tribe of Eliyahu, are bound to this 'reishis', the land of the future. Their sheep were lofty souls, which Moshe knew. The Mashgiach closes that the Three Weeks are days of digging for hidden kedushah through Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

en: According to the Sfas Emes, the land east of the Jordan was truly the portion of Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad; their fault was only that they hurried to take it instead of waiting for it to be given al pi haTorah.

A person's nefesh extends into his belongings, and Hashem's hashgachah gives each person exactly what is his; one who grabs his portion dishonestly would have received it anyway, and loses it because he hurried.

Of the ten maamaros the first three are beyond human grasp, and likewise of the ten nations promised to Avraham the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni are not yet accessible; they will become Klal Yisrael's when Moshiach comes.

The ten weeks before Rosh Hashanah parallel the ten nations: the Three Weeks correspond to the hidden Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, and the seven weeks of consolation to the seven nations already conquered.
Reuven, the firstborn, is 'reishis', and Gad is the tribe of Eliyahu and the geulah; both are bound to the days of Moshiach, which is why they wanted this land.
The Mashgiach explains that their great livestock were lofty souls of the future, and Moshe Rabbeinu's 'I know' means that he knew their secret, though they should not have put it into words.
The Three Weeks are days of digging: through extra effort in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah one can uncover the kedushah hidden beneath their darkness.

title.en: Why 'I know' and why 'atzum me'od'

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke that Bnei Gad and Bnei Reuven put their sheep before their children, and asks why Moshe says 'I know you have much livestock' and why the Torah stresses 'atzum me'od'. He brings the Midrash that they hurried for their portion and were the first exiled, and the Sfas Emes that the portion was truly theirs but should have come al pi haTorah.

title.en: What is yours will come to you

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person's nefesh extends into his belongings, and that Hashem divides everything with exactness so each gets what is his, illustrated with a cup of soda. One who uses dishonest means for something would have gotten it anyway, and because he hurried he loses it; so too Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad.

title.en: The ten maamaros and the hidden first three

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that the world was created with ten maamaros and the Gemara that 'Bereishis' is also a maamar, showing how lofty it is. The first three are beyond our grasp and are heavenly, while the last seven are earthly and familiar to us.

title.en: Keini, Kenizi, Kadmoni: kedushah under tumah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that of the ten nations promised to Avraham, the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni (Ammon, Moav and Esav) are mentioned only once and will be Klal Yisrael's only in the days of Moshiach. They are covered by a great tumah like an orlah, and following the Sfas Emes and the Chesed L'Avraham their hidden kedushah is greater than that of Eretz Yisrael proper; the land of Reuven and Gad was a piece of Ammon and Moav taken through Sichon.

title.en: The Three Weeks as the hidden three lands

summary.en: The Mashgiach maps the ten weeks before Rosh Hashanah onto the ten nations: the seven weeks of consolation are graspable, while the Three Weeks are the Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni and will be the most joyful days when Moshiach comes. He brings the Avodas Yisrael on 'kol rodfeha hisiguha bein hametzarim', says learning and davening are harder now but reach higher, and gives a mashal of embroidery on a black cloth.

title.en: Reuven the firstborn and Gad of Eliyahu

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the hidden world of the first three is the source of good concealed in suffering, pointing to the Igeres HaKodesh. He then explains that Reuven, as bechor, is 'reishis' but lost the bechorah through haste; in the time of tikun every blemish will be washed out and he will regain it. Gad too is bound to Moshiach, since Eliyahu comes from Gad.

title.en: Gad saw 'reishis'; half of Menashe

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Vezos Habrachah that Gad 'saw reishis' because Moshe is buried there, and adds that they wanted Moshe's conquest rather than Yehoshua's. Gimmel-Reish of the first three stands for Gad and Reuven, and the half tribe of Menashe, who also lost a bechorah, joins them; Esav, the third, remains untouchable until Moshiach.

title.en: Rashi's 'koach maasav' and the Kadmoni

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's question why the Torah begins with Bereishis and the answer 'koach maasav higid l'amo', and the passuk that the saviors will judge Har Esav. He explains that Esav is the klipah over the kedushah of Bereishis, so the Torah's opening hints that Klal Yisrael will one day receive the Kadmoni and the whole world; the answer to the nations is that their complaint over the seven nations misses the point.

title.en: The forty days of the spies and Tammuz

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Shimshon of Ostropoli on 'vehayamim yemei bikurei anavim': the letters before 'anavim' spell the name of the Samech Mem, so these forty days, Tammuz and the nine days, are in his domain. He supports that the nine days belong to Tammuz from the Chasam Sofer and the Bnei Yissaschar, and adds gematrios linking these days to Har Esav and the Kadmoni.

title.en: Souls of the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says such lofty matters must be learned by way of drush, and proposes that Bnei Reuven and Bnei Gad were souls of the days of Moshiach, so their instincts told them, as the Sfas Emes says, that this land was theirs. He compares it to belief in techiyas hameisim being a sign of having a share in it, and explains Moshe's 'I know' as 'I know your secret'.

title.en: Yaakov's sheep and the Yismach Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that Yaakov's sheep were holy souls he drew out of Lavan's domain, and tells how the Yismach Moshe remembered his earlier gilgulim, including the dispute of Korach and being a sheep of Yaakov Avinu. From this and the Midrash on Yaakov's 600,000 flocks he concludes that the livestock of these tribes were lofty souls of the future.

title.en: Hidden light: 'I found David in Sedom'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Moshe's words: he knew how great their sheep were, but they should not have said it openly. He then says hidden good lies in the Three Weeks: Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av, Shiva Asar B'Tammuz is destined to be a 'chag', and the Midrash finds David in Sedom, with great souls hidden under refuse. He calls these forty days of digging for kedushah.

title.en: Yovel at the end of Bamidbar and the avodah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the word yovel, meaning return to the root, appears twenty-one times in the Torah, the last at the end of Bamidbar, and follows the tzaddikim's custom of finding a hint that Moshiach comes this year. He closes that Tammuz and Rosh Chodesh Menachem Av hint to Melech HaMashiach and calls for hard work in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah in these weeks.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Eliyahu HaNavi, though from the tribe of Binyamin, is called a kohen, and how lighting the Chanukah candles and a bris bring every Jew into the state of a kohen, as it will be in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Harachaman of a bris that calls Eliyahu HaNavi 'kohen tzedek', and asks how one may pray with a title that is not true. The Midrash disputes whether Eliyahu was from Gad or Binyamin, and Eliyahu himself said he descends from Rachel. When asked in the Gemara why he stood in a cemetery of gentiles if he is a kohen, he answered with Rabbi Shimon's view, which we do not follow; Tosafos says he was only deflecting. The Mashgiach then brings that Chanukah lights keep their power all year and make the home a Beis HaMikdash, and explains that the lighter becomes a kohen, since the light of Moshiach is revealed and in the future every Jew will be a kohen. Eliyahu, who always lives in the atmosphere of Moshiach, is therefore always a kohen and paskens like Rabbi Shimon. He ends with the bris as a korban and blessings for the family.

en: Eliyahu HaNavi was not a kohen by lineage: he himself said he descends from Rachel, and Tosafos says his answer about Rabbi Shimon's view was only a deflection.
The power and impression of the Chanukah lights remain in the home all year, and the Jewish home becomes a Beis HaMikdash.
The Mashgiach explains that whoever lights Chanukah candles becomes a kohen, because the light of Moshiach is revealed then and in the future every Jew will be a kohen.
Eliyahu, the herald of the redemption, always lives in the state of the days of Moshiach, so he is always a kohen and rules like Rabbi Shimon as the halacha will be in the future.
A bris is like a korban, and when Eliyahu comes to it he brings the atmosphere of Moshiach, so every Jew there carries a spark of kehunah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every generation's new answer to how the first night of Chanukah was a miracle draws down a new salvation, and that for our empty, fallen generation the miracle is lit even from an empty flask with only a trace of oil left on its walls.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the repetition, in Parshas Beha'aloscha, of how the menorah was made as one beaten piece, and turns to the well-known question of what the miracle of the first night was. He brings the Tzvi LaTzaddik and the Yismach Yisroel, who answer that the flask found was empty, holding only drops left on its walls. Asking how a new answer can differ from all the Rishonim, he explains through the Mishnah in Niddah and the Arizal that each Torah view reflects its own heavenly heichal, and that each chacham's chiddush on the Chanukah miracle draws down a new salvation. Chanukah, he says, is above all for the lowly later generations, which are like empty ears of grain. Leaders shrink, yet Hashem can be served in every situation, and today a sigh of teshuvah counts as much as great fasts did once. In our generation there is no flask, only a trace of oil, and that suffices. On Zos Chanukah he explains the menorah as one piece, joining even its base, the souls of the end of days, to its lights.

en: The Tzvi LaTzaddik and the Yismach Yisroel answer that the flask the Chashmona'im found was empty, used before for oil, and the few drops left on it made even the first night a miracle.
Each Torah view comes from its own heichal in Heaven according to the root of the scholar's soul, and the psak decided below shapes reality in this world.
Every chacham's new answer to how the Chanukah miracle happened draws down a new salvation in his generation.
Chanukah is mainly for the later, lower generations, who are like empty ears of grain, and its light comes down to them.
Following the Beis Aharon and the Ba'al Shem Tov, Hashem can and must be served in every situation, with whatever one has.
In today's small generations a sigh of teshuvah or a resolution to improve is as great before Hashem as the hard avodah of earlier times.
The menorah, made as one beaten piece down to its base, shows that all of Klal Yisroel, even the souls of the end of days, are one with its shining lights.

title.en: The menorah as one beaten piece, and the first-night question

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Parshas Beha'aloscha repeats how the menorah was made, stressing that it is one beaten piece, unlike Terumah where broken pieces could be refined and reused. He then raises the question of what the miracle of the first night was and introduces the Tzvi LaTzaddik's new answer, which he says he would not have given had it not been the truth.

title.en: The empty flask: Tzvi LaTzaddik and Yismach Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tzvi LaTzaddik's answer: the flask with the Kohen Gadol's seal was empty, a flask once used for oil, and from the few drops left on it the light burned even on the first night. He notes the same answer in the Yismach Yisroel and asks why it is called a path the Rishonim did not take.

title.en: Many true answers: the heichalos above

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how many conflicting answers can all be true, and brings the Mishnah in Niddah where Rashi, Tosafos and the Rambam explain differently and the Chasam Sofer writes that reality matches only the Rambam. He answers with the Arizal and the Beis Yosef on the shape of the letters, and with the teaching that in Heaven there are many heichalos, each learning Torah according to its own middos.

title.en: Psak shapes reality; each answer brings a new salvation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rashi and Tosafos each spoke from their own root, while the Rambam as a posek matched this world, and that reality follows the psak. So every chacham who answers the Beis Yosef's question draws down a new kind of miracle in his generation. He adds that Chanukah is mainly for the later generations and for those too low to rise to Shabbos.

title.en: Falling generations and the empty ears of grain

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the lower the generation falls, the nearer Moshiach comes, citing 'nafla velo sosif' and the Chessed l'Avraham. Today's generations are like Pharaoh's empty ears of grain, and as Yosef brought plenty into the years of famine, Chanukah sweetens the season of Teves. He describes the emptiness of the individual compared with the avodah of earlier generations.

title.en: Shrinking leaders; serving Hashem in every situation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the navi was once called ro'eh because a look from the tzaddik was enough, later speech was needed, and today even speech does not help. He brings the Beis Aharon's Yiddish teaching that no creature can raise itself to serve G-d except as He wills, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's lesson that one serves Hashem in every circumstance, even with confusion during davening.

title.en: Stories: locked in, and a teaching that lasted three years

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man locked in a place where one may not think words of Torah, who knocked on the walls for hours so as not to think Torah, as his way of serving Hashem there. He then tells of a chassid who came to the Beis Aharon after three years because one short teaching had sustained him until then, and the Rebbe wrote it down.

title.en: Then and now: a sigh of teshuvah suffices

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells, as heard from the Skverer Rebbe, of a boy who rested from learning by learning complex Mishnayos and Hilchos Kiddush HaChodesh, and did not know what playing meant; such children no longer grow today. He brings the Beis Aharon on 'dor ledor yeshabach' and the Arizal's answer about Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's fast: in small generations a sigh to Hashem counts as much.

title.en: No flask today, only a trace of oil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that earlier generations still had a pure flask, often a tzaddik of the generation, but today there is not even that, only a little oil clinging to the walls. In our generation, he says, the chachamim revealed a new Chanukah miracle from an empty flask, and the seal that remains is the point of emunah of Avraham Avinu, whom the Midrash calls a Kohen Gadol, which no Greek can defile.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the empty eighth light

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al HaTanya that the lights reach even the 'feet', those who still long for Hashem. He explains that the eighth light stood empty all of Chanukah and is lit only now, that each night corresponds to one of the thirteen middos of mercy, and that the gathering in shul allows lighting even later.

title.en: The menorah as all of Klal Yisroel, one piece

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on the eighth day Beha'aloscha is read because the menorah includes all of Klal Yisroel and the whole Torah. The seven shepherds shine at its top, and its base is the souls of the end of days, yet all is one beaten piece. He says this parsha speaks of the Chanukah menorah and so repeats that even the base is mikshah.

title.en: Gam yachad: gathering as one, and a prayer for the end

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the psalm said before lighting, 'Hinei mah tov… gam yachad': the Chanukah gathering is itself mikshah, and the good oil flows from the head to the beard, the thirteen middos. He closes with a prayer that the empty souls of the end of days be helped and the whole menorah be complete.

oneLiner.en: At the seudah of Zos Chanukah the Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon and the kohanim, the day of hod and hallel, on which every Jew, by lighting his candles, builds a piece of the menorah of the Beis Hamikdash that Moshiach will bring down.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's question why the menorah follows the offerings of the nesi'im, and with the Ramban's answer that Aharon's portion is the Chanukah lights. Chanukah is therefore the Yom Tov of Aharon and the kohanim, when every Jewish home becomes a Beis Hamikdash, and its eight lights correspond to the names of Moshiach. The seudah of Zos Chanukah strengthens the emunah in Moshiach and the waiting for him. Aharon is the middah of hod, and so Chanukah is the day of thanks and hallel; the Mashgiach connects Hallel to Aharon's years and to the Beis Hamikdash. Each generation, lighting its candles, builds a part of the menorah of the third Beis Hamikdash: the great generations the cups and flowers, our low generation the base, all one hammered piece, as the Tanya teaches of all souls. He closes with the chasimah of Zos Chanukah and a tefilah for the redemption.

en: Following the Ramban, the Mashgiach explains that Aharon's consolation was the Chanukah lights, so Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon and the kohanim.
Through the Chanukah lights Aharon inaugurates every Jewish home as a Beis Hamikdash.
The seudah of Zos Chanukah is meant to strengthen the emunah in Moshiach and the hope for the yeshuah.
Aharon is the middah of hod, and Chanukah, which is in hod, is the day of thanks and Hallel.
Every generation, by lighting Chanukah candles, builds a part of the menorah of the future Beis Hamikdash, which will come down from Heaven when it is complete.
The lowest generations make the base of the menorah, yet the menorah is one hammered piece, binding the lowest Jew to the highest.

He explains why the Torah gives Aharon's age and date of passing in Parshas Masei: there Aharon stands for the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Tzemach, ma'alin bakodesh, and one hammered menorah

summary.en: From the Chanukah haftorah, 'Behold I bring My servant Tzemach', the Mashgiach explains that lighting brings Moshiach like a hidden sprout, and that 'beha'aloscha' hints to adding a new light each day. Our low generations make the base of the menorah, yet as the Tanya says all souls are bound together: the menorah is one hammered piece from base to flowers.

title.en: Zos Chanukah, the day of the seal

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the reading of Zos Chanukah, of a world called Klal Yisrael where all souls are equal, and of Aharon who did not change. He explains that Zos Chanukah is the day of the chasimah, which each Jew makes through his own avodah of the Chanukah lights, and closes with a tefilah for the redemption.

catalogTitle: The Lesson of the בני מכיר and the בנות צלפחד: Our Eternal Connection to Eretz Yisroel

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew, like every shidduch, is drawn back to his origin in Eretz Yisrael, and that the Bnei Machir and the daughters of Tzelafchad, the family that held Gilad, carry the law of return that Eliyahu will announce at the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Moshe, in Sefer Devarim, retells that he gave Gilad to Machir, something the people saw only months before. He links three episodes about the family of Machir: their conquest of Gilad, the daughters of Tzelafchad's request for a nachalah, and the complaint of the Bnei Machir that ends Bamidbar. The daughters waited forty years for a fitting match and are praised, while Nadav and Avihu are criticized for the same; the Mashgiach explains through the principle that everything is drawn to its origin: the isha to the ish, Adam to the earth of the mizbeach and Eretz Yisrael. Once the daughters received a nachalah they were joined to their root and found their shidduch at once. Gilad, the land of Eliyahu HaGiladi, is the place of Yovel, the law of return, which only Rachel's children could conquer. He ends that Shabbos Chazon is a Shabbos of hope and a great eis ratzon.

en: Everything is drawn back to its origin: the isha to the ish she came from, and Adam to the earth of the mizbeach from which he was formed.
The Mashgiach explains that a person with a pure heart can rely on the inclination of his heart in choosing a shidduch, because it draws him to his true match.
The daughters of Tzelafchad found their shidduch only after they received a nachalah, because that joined them to Eretz Yisrael, the root of their root.
Yovel is the law of return, and Eliyahu HaNavi, who lived in Gilad, is the one who will announce the great return of Klal Yisrael.
Gilad, the land of return, could be conquered only by Rachel's children, which is why Moshe left it for the Bnei Machir of Menashe.
Shabbos Chazon is not only a Shabbos of sorrow; the Mashgiach calls it a Shabbos of hope, when the heart can see the third Beis HaMikdash, and a great eis ratzon.
