title.en: Why Moshe retells recent events

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Moshe's recounting to the new generation at the start of Sefer Devarim, and asks what purpose there is in telling them about the war with Sichon and Og and the giving of Gilad, events that happened only five or six months earlier.

title.en: The complaint of the Bnei Machir

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the complaint at the end of Bamidbar: the family of Machir feared that the daughters of Tzelafchad would marry into another shevet and their nachalah would pass out of Menashe, and Moshe tells them they are right. He notes this is the third episode involving this family, after Gilad and the daughters' own request for a nachalah.

title.en: Waiting forty years: praised or criticized?

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the three episodes together and brings the Midrash that the daughters of Tzelafchad waited forty years for a fitting match and are praised for it. He contrasts this with Chazal's criticism of Nadav and Avihu for not marrying because no one was good enough, and asks how the two fit together.

title.en: The match under their nose; the heart decides

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that the daughters finally married their own cousins, who lived nearby all along, and insists nothing happens by chance. He brings a letter answering someone torn between two shidduchim: no one today can decide for him, but Hashem guides through the inclination of the heart.

title.en: Everything is drawn to its origin

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the heart should decide a shidduch and answers with the law that everything is drawn to its origin, contrasting the Torah's view with Newton's gravity. The isha comes from the ish, and Adam from the earth of the mizbeach, so a match is a reunion; this explains the Gemara that the mizbeach weeps over one who divorces his first wife, and why one should follow a pure heart.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, the root of the root

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew belongs to Eretz Yisrael and must return there, and that one cut off from his wife is cut off from Eretz Yisrael too, as hinted in the first Mishnah of Gittin. The daughters of Tzelafchad, as tzidkaniyos, relied on their heart, which drew them to no one until their nachalah tied them to Eretz Yisrael; then their shidduch appeared. The parsha read before Chodesh Av repairs the sin of the meraglim, who did not long for the eretz chemdah.

title.en: Why Moshe did not take Gilad

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Bnei Machir, who went to Gilad and drove out the Emori there. He explains that Amon and Moav were off-limits, and Moshe could take their former land only because Sichon had conquered it, and asks why Moshe stopped short of Gilad and left it for the Bnei Machir.

title.en: Kiryas Sefer and the forgotten halachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Kalev's promise to whoever would conquer Kiryas Sefer, and the Gemara in Temurah that Osniel ben Kenaz restored the three thousand halachos forgotten in the days of mourning for Moshe. He cites an explanation that the Torah is written into the land of Eretz Yisrael, so that conquering a piece of land gave Osniel a connection to the halachos hidden in it.

title.en: Gilad and Yovel, the law of return

summary.en: The Mashgiach proposes that Gilad is connected to the parsha of Yovel, the law of return. Land in Eretz Yisrael that is bought returns to its owner, because it belongs to his neshamah; the eved who took a shifchah that is not his goes free at Yovel. Every Jew, wherever he is, will return to Yerushalayim and the place of the mizbeach, and he cites the Arizal that even very sinful souls will eventually return.

title.en: Eliyahu HaGiladi, herald of the return

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Eliyahu HaNavi is the herald of Yovel who will return children to parents and Klal Yisrael to Hashem and to Eretz Yisrael, and that Yovel and teshuvah are one. Eliyahu chose to live in Gilad, the land of Yovel, and brought the people back to Hashem at Har HaCarmel. He then asks why Moshe did not fight Amalek himself.

title.en: Rachel's children, Amalek and Gilad

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that only Rachel's children can overcome Amalek, so Moshe, from Levi, sent Yehoshua. Purim will not be nullified because Amalek was never fully erased; that will come with Moshiach. Rachel is the neshamah of return, as the navi promises her that her children will return, and therefore only her children, Menashe's family of Machir, could conquer Gilad, the land of return that Moshe left over.

title.en: Shabbos Chazon: a Shabbos of hope

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that Shabbos Chazon is not what it seems on the surface: beyond the sorrow, it is the Shabbos before what Tisha B'Av is meant to become, the greatest moed. He brings that on Shabbos Chazon Hashem shows each Jew the third Beis HaMikdash, each according to how much he felt the mourning for Yerushalayim, and that the heart can see.

title.en: Sefer Devarim: Torah for the seventy exiles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Sefer Devarim, begun on this Shabbos, is a book of return rather than separation. He asks why Moshe explained the Torah in seventy languages a month before his passing, and, through the wagons Yosef sent, connects the number seventy to galus. Moshe prepared the people for the seventieth, lowest level of galus by bringing the Torah down into every language, so that it would go down with them as a comfort.

title.en: Machir and Gilad: the answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his opening question: Moshe retold that he gave Gilad to Machir as a comfort, because Machir and Gilad stand for return and redemption at the end of galus, where Eliyahu HaGiladi will emerge. This is why only the Bnei Machir complained that a nachalah must not leave its shevet, and why the daughters of Tzelafchad married into Machir and received Gilad.

title.en: The great eis ratzon of Shabbos Chazon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Shabbos afternoon is a great eis ratzon even though the afternoon is otherwise a time of din, and says that Shabbos Chazon, amid the days of din, is entirely one great eis ratzon. He urges using every moment of it and closes with a brachah that Tisha B'Av turn to joy.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Chanukah menorah is one piece with eight lamps: its lit and empty lamps hold both sides of the miracle, salvation for the Jews and downfall for the nations, until on Zos Chanukah all eight are full.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk in Beha'aloscha about Aharon lighting the Menorah and its being 'mikshah', and asks why the Torah repeats this. He then asks why the minhag is one menorah of eight lamps rather than a separate lamp each night. From the Gemara's two versions of the Chanukah brachah he draws two sides of the miracle: salvation for Klal Yisrael and downfall of the nations, matching Beis Hillel's increasing and Beis Shammai's decreasing lights. Through the Arizal on the eight kings of Edom and the Bnei Yissaschar, he explains that the oil lasted because the 'long days' of Moshiach shone, so all eight lamps stand from the first night. The full lamps are the Jews and the empty ones the nations. A bracha cannot be made over empty vessels, so the menorah must be one piece. On Zos Chanukah, like Shemini Atzeres, all eight are full. He closes with a story about emunah and a brachah.

en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah repeats the making of the Menorah in Beha'aloscha, mentioning only that it is mikshah, one piece, and why Jews use one menorah of eight lamps instead of separate lamps.
The miracle has two sides, the downfall of the enemies and the salvation of Israel, reflected in the two versions of the brachah and in Beis Shammai's and Beis Hillel's ways of lighting.
The oil burned eight days because the 'long days' of Moshiach shone at that time, so a menorah of eight branches stands even on the first night to show that one day stretched into eight.
The lit lamps represent Klal Yisrael, growing brighter each night, and the dark empty lamps the nations, growing fewer.
The menorah must be one piece because a brachah is not made over empty vessels; as one piece with a lit lamp, its empty lamps are not an empty vessel.
Zos Chanukah is like Shemini Atzeres: all eight lamps are full, none empty, and the light of Moshiach is fully revealed.

summary.en: From the Gemara in Megillah on the two versions of the brachah, the Mashgiach shows that the miracle was both vengeance on the enemies and salvation for Israel, like the plagues in Egypt that were healing for the Jews. He ties the two sides to Beis Shammai's decreasing and Beis Hillel's increasing lights, then recalls Megillas Taanis on the twenty-fifth of Kislev.

title.en: Long days of Moshiach in eight lamps

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal on the eight kings of Edom: after the long exile of Edom will come days of Moshiach that are long days. Following the Bnei Yissaschar, Chanukah prepares for Moshiach, and the oil lasted because a day of 'orech yamim' came. This is why a menorah of eight branches stands from the first night.

title.en: Aharon prepared the Chanukah menorah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why eight separate lamps would not suffice, and brings the Ramban that Aharon's Menorah alludes to Chanukah. Through his unchanging avodah Aharon drew down the light of Moshiach and prepared the Chashmonaim's menorah and ours, so 'ken asah' refers to the Chanukah menorah. He links this to Nachshon ben Aminadav, root of Moshiach.

title.en: Chanukah as a continuation of Sukkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sfas Emes that Chanukah continues Sukkos, whose decreasing bulls were offered for the nations. So the Chanukah lights, too, give the nations some share, and this is Beis Shammai's decreasing order. Both views are correct, and the two versions of the brachah match them.

title.en: Full lamps and empty lamps

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the menorah is made of lit, full lamps and dark, empty ones: the full are Klal Yisrael, growing each night, and the empty are the nations, growing fewer. Like Egypt's darkness while the Jews had light, both are in the menorah. The seven dark lamps correspond to the seven kings of Edom of whom the Torah says 'vayamos'.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and why mikshah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Zos Chanukah to Shemini Atzeres, which comes after seven days, when all eight strings of Moshiach's harp play. He then answers why the menorah must be mikshah: a brachah is not made over an empty vessel, and as one piece with a lit lamp the empty lamps are not an empty vessel. The empty lamps are as much a mitzvah as the full ones.

title.en: Tonight all eight lamps are full

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that today, Zos Chanukah, the twenty-fifth of Kislev reaches completion: all eight lamps are full, none empty, and the nations have no part, like Shemini Atzeres. Aharon's avodah gave Jews a menorah holding darkness and light, and 'ken asah' speaks of every Jew's menorah. Tonight all eight lights are holy, a good sign.

title.en: Believing in the light of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Jews look at the menorah and believe the light of Moshiach shines from it, and tells of a tzaddik who saw the ushpizin and the Kotzker who answered that believing they come is greater. He closes with a brachah for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Matisyahu ben Yochanan's name marks the soul that knows everything it receives is an undeserved gift from Hashem, and that Chanukah, and above all Zos Chanukah, teaches that even nature is a miracle.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Al HaNissim names Matisyahu together with his father, unlike Mordechai on Purim. He brings the Gemara that the world is sustained for the sake of Chanina, and explains that in every generation there is a soul called 'Chanina', who knows nothing is due to him and that all he receives is chesed. Moshe, the humblest of men, and Yaakov, the man of truth, saw themselves this way. Matisyahu ('a gift of Yud-Kei-Vav') ben Yochanan carries the same idea. From the story of Rabbi Chanina's daughter, whose vinegar burned like oil, the Mashgiach explains that for one who sees everything as a gift, nature and miracle are the same. Through Chasam Sofer's picture of the generation that saw manna and then bread from the earth, he teaches that nature is only a veil. Chanukah, the last mitzvah given, seals emunah, and through emunah Moshiach will come.

en: In every generation there is a soul called 'Chanina' who knows that nothing is owed to him and that everything he receives is Hashem's chesed, and the world is sustained for his sake.
The name Matisyahu ben Yochanan expresses this awareness: 'Matisyahu' is a gift of Yud-Kei-Vav, and 'Yochanan' contains 'chanan', grace.
For one who sees everything as a gift, there is no difference between oil burning and vinegar burning: everything is equally a miracle.
Nature is only a veil over G-dliness; a Jew bound to Hashem sees G-dliness in fire, in a tree and in a wall.
The eighth day, Zos Chanukah, taught that even oil burning by nature is a miracle, and that Hashem runs the world.
Chanukah is the last of the mitzvos given, so the count of mitzvos begins with emunah (Anochi) and ends with emunah, and in the merit of emunah Moshiach will come.

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Moshe Rabbeinu, the humblest of men, davened only for a free gift, and that Yaakov, the man of truth, knew nothing was due to him. He then explains Matisyahu ben Yochanan's name, like Mordechai ben Yair's, as describing the soul: a gift of Yud-Kei-Vav and grace.

title.en: Oil or vinegar: all is a miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one who sees Chanina, Chananiah or Yochanan in a dream will see miracles, and the story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's daughter, whose vinegar burned all Shabbos. He asks how Rabbi Chanina could rely on a miracle, and answers that for one who knows every breath is a gift, oil burning and vinegar burning are the same miracle.

title.en: Manna, bread and the veil of nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's picture of the generation born in the desert, who were amazed when bread grew from the earth, and explains that bread from the earth is as wondrous as bread from heaven. He mocks the scientist who thinks 'gravity' explains anything, and teaches that nature is only a veil; one who cleaves to Hashem sees G-dliness in everything, as the Ba'al Shem Tov taught.

title.en: Emunah is planting; the few Chashmonaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who dreams of Chanina sees miracles in every bite and breath, and that emunah is 'Zeraim' because a Jew plants knowing that the growth is a miracle, unlike a gentile who is used to it. The Chashmonaim, a handful of people, went to war on the level of Matisyahu ben Yochanan, knowing everything comes from Hashem.

title.en: Zos Chanukah and the seal of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer on the miracle of the first day, and explains that after seven days of miracles the Jews recognized that even the naturally burning oil of the eighth day, Zos Chanukah, was a miracle. Chanukah, the last mitzvah given, closes the mitzvos that began with Anochi, giving the last generation emunah, and in its merit Moshiach will come; he ends with a brachah.

title.en: Stories at the table: sweeping the beis medrash

summary.en: Stories are told at the table, among them a chassid who swept a beis medrash at night to serve a visiting tzaddik, and Reb Hersh, the attendant of Reb Mendel of Rimanov, whose sweeping cleared away foreign thoughts before davening.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is the Yom Tov of Aharon HaKohen: through the Chanukah lights Aharon's lighting of the Menorah continues in every Jew, bringing his middah of hod, thanksgiving, peace and the hidden light.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that Aharon was told his share is greater than the Nesi'im's, since he lights the Menorah, and with the Ramban that this hints at the Chanukah miracle of the Chashmona'im. Building on the Sfas Emes and the Chasam Sofer, he explains that on Chanukah every Jew performs the Temple service and becomes like a kohen. Using the Arizal's teaching that a tzaddik's soul joins whoever does his favorite mitzvah, he explains that Aharon, who never changed in his lighting, is revealed in every Jew who lights. Hoda'ah, he says, is Aharon's middah of hod. He then explains why Zos Chanukah is the final sealing of judgment: the light of Chanukah is the hidden light, and a Jew is judged by the hidden good within him, as the Chozeh of Lublin story shows. He connects shalom bayis, which outweighs the Chanukah light, to Aharon the lover of peace, speaks of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, and closes by urging the year-round thanking of Hashem in the morning davening.

en: The Mashgiach explains, following the Sfas Emes and the Chasam Sofer, that the Chanukah lights are the one remnant of the Temple service left today, so for eight days every Jew becomes like a kohen.
Since Aharon never changed in his lighting, his soul joins every Jew who lights the Chanukah candles with the proper intention, so his lighting lasts forever.
The essence of Chanukah is hallel and hoda'ah, and hoda'ah is the middah of hod, which is Aharon and the Bais HaMikdash.
Zos Chanukah is the final sealing because the Chanukah light is the hidden light, and on it a Jew is judged by the hidden good within him rather than by his deeds.
Shalom bayis outweighs even the Chanukah light because Chanukah is Aharon's Yom Tov, and Aharon loved and pursued peace.
From Chanukah one draws hoda'ah for the whole year: thanking Hashem for His constant supervision and for the daily hidden miracles, above all in the morning davening.

With the Arizal's teaching, illustrated by the story of the Midrash Shmuel and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, that a tzaddik's soul joins one who does his mitzvah, he explains that Aharon's soul joins every Jew who lights Chanukah candles, so his lighting is forever.

title.en: Hallel and hoda'ah: Aharon's middah of hod

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah, in Kislev and Teves, stands above the order of months, and that each Jew received a spark of Aharon's soul. Chanukah's essence is hallel and hoda'ah; hoda'ah is hod, which is Aharon and the Bais HaMikdash, and Chanukah trains a Jew to thank Hashem for everything.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as the final sealing; the Lubliner story

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Bas Ayin, in the name of the Arizal, that the final sealing is on Zos Chanukah, and asks what this gives a person who did not do real teshuvah. He tells the story, from the Imrei Emes and the Shem MiShmuel, of an informer whose kvittel the Chozeh of Lublin first could not act on because the man's soul was shining while he lit Chanukah candles.

title.en: The hidden light and judgment by inner good

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the story with the Bnei Yissaschar: the Chanukah light is the hidden light of Moshiach, hidden in every Jew. On Chanukah a Jew is judged by that light rather than by his deeds, as Moshiach will find merit in the worst Jew according to Rabbi Gedalia of Linitz; so even a little teshuvah suffices, which explains the Ruzhiner's saying about Zos Chanukah.

title.en: Shalom bayis outweighs the Chanukah light

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara's rule that the Shabbos light comes before the Chanukah light because of shalom bayis is where the Rambam praises peace. He explains it with the Meiri: Shabbos lights are the wife's mitzvah and Chanukah lights the husband's. Chanukah is Aharon's Yom Tov, and Aharon loved and pursued peace, so the greatness of shalom bayis was revealed through the Chanukah light.

title.en: The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy on Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from the Arizal, via the Bnei Yissaschar, that the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy come down over the days of Chanukah and are complete on the eighth day. He connects this to the passuk of the oil running down Aharon's beard, and says each Yom Tov gives a middah for the year: from Chanukah, hod.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for His constant supervision

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Modim thanks for 'our lives entrusted in Your hand': Hashem supervises every step Himself. With the Ramban he says one who believes that everything is a miracle thanks Hashem constantly. He urges beginning the day with praise in the morning davening, explaining the passuk of the crucible: praise of Hashem purifies a person and opens the light of Torah. He closes with a tefilah that, on the last day of Chanukah, all should feel the sweetness of praising Hashem and that Chanukah should prepare for the day that is all Shabbos.

catalogTitle: “נשלחה אנשים לפנינו” - The Importance of Being a שליח of 'ה

oneLiner.en: Starting from the two accounts of who sent the meraglim, the Mashgiach teaches that every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem with a personal mission hidden in his name, and that in the days of Tammuz and Av, and in the end of days, he must hold on to emunah and remember whose shaliach he is.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Parshas Devarim says the people asked to send spies while Parshas Shelach says Hashem commanded it. He brings the Chasam Sofer: the power of the sender rests in the agent, and the people's bad intentions spoiled the mission. The Mashgiach reverses it: the people asked first, and Hashem joined as a sender so the meraglim would at least have a choice, which saved Kalev and Yehoshua. From here he explains that every Jew doing a mitzvah is Hashem's shaliach; each has a unique mission carried in his name, and the yetzer hara's own mission is to make him forget it. Tammuz and Av are the days of the Samech-Mem's power, but under the deepest tumah lies the greatest kedusha. The meraglim's sin was going by reason instead of emunah. Tzitzis, at the bottom of the garment, is the reminder for the end of days. He closes with Hashem's love for every Jew and the vision of the third Beis HaMikdash on Shabbos Chazon.

en: Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that the power and intention of the sender pass into the agent, so the people's flawed intention harmed the meraglim, just as a congregation's intentions affect its shliach tzibbur.
Every Jew who does a mitzvah because Hashem commanded it is Hashem's shaliach and carries His power.
Each person comes into the world with a unique mission that is carried in his name, and the yetzer hara's own mission is to make him forget it.
Tammuz and Av are days when the Samech-Mem has special power, and correcting the sin of the meraglim means holding on to emunah in these days.
The greater the kedusha, the more it is covered with tumah, so the days of Bein HaMetzarim hide the greatest potential for closeness to Hashem.
Tzitzis is the remedy for the end of days: it reminds a Jew whose shaliach he is.
Hashem loves every Jew, even the worst, and one must not let the Satan persuade him otherwise.

summary.en: The Mashgiach offers two readings: Hashem took the blame on Himself in Shelach, or, as the Mashgiach prefers, the people asked first and Hashem added Himself as a sender so His intention would count too. This gave the meraglim a choice and saved Kalev and Yehoshua.

title.en: Every Jew is Hashem's shaliach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew who does a mitzvah is Hashem's shaliach and carries His power, illustrated by the scribe who may not sit on one bench with the Sefer Torah he wrote. When a Jew forgets his mission, Hashem sends him thoughts of teshuvah, which a busy person brushes off.

summary.en: Picturing people rushing along a New York avenue, the Mashgiach asks whose shaliach each one is: Hashem's or his yetzer's. He explains that shlichus needs a neshama that is a part of G-d, that it was first given with the korban Pesach when the Jews became a people, and that Moshe wanted the meraglim to carry this G-dly power of shlichus.

title.en: A person's mission is in his name

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shelah's practice of saying a passuk for one's name at the end of Shemoneh Esrei, and explains that each Jew has a unique mission carried in his name, citing Rashi that angels' names change with their mission and the Arizal on a father's naming. Leaving Shemoneh Esrei for the marketplace, one easily forgets his mission, and the passuk reminds him.

title.en: The angel's answer and the names in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the angel answered Yaakov's 'tell me your name' with 'why do you ask my name', and explains that this was his true answer: the mission of the Satan is to make a person not ask his own name. Likewise the Torah repeats the names of Bnei Yisrael going down to Mitzrayim, in Vayigash and again in Shemos, so they would not forget their mission there.

title.en: The meraglim's names and the days of bikurei anavim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah repeats the meraglim's names to remind them they were Moshe's shluchim, not agents of their own interests, which the Zohar describes. Their mission fell in Tammuz and Av, the season of the Samech-Mem's power, hinted in 'yemei bikurei anavim': the letters before those of 'anavim' spell the Satan's name.

title.en: Amalek in the Negev: reason against emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev' as the power of the Samech-Mem in these dry days, and that the three weeks and nine days exist to correct the sin of the meraglim. He says the meraglim were right by reason that they could not conquer the land; their sin was going with reason instead of with emunah.

title.en: Hidden kedusha and Moshiach in Tammuz and Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the higher the kedusha, the more it is covered by tumah, so in Bein HaMetzarim one can reach more than at any other time, and these days will be the greatest festivals when Moshiach comes. Moshiach is hidden in them, born on Tisha B'Av, and Tammuz and Menachem Av are in gematria 'Melech HaMashiach'. Shelach ends with tzitzis as the reminder of one's mission.

title.en: Acharis hayamim and the tzitzis at the edge

summary.en: Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach calls the three weeks the 'end of the days' of the year, matching the end of days in history, the heels of Moshiach, when Jews have fallen lower than ever, kept afloat only by Torah. Tzitzis, which reminded the student in the Gemara Menachos who he was, hang at the bottom of the garment, and Moshe saw his people struggling to swim to the shore of Moshiach.

title.en: Weaving the garment of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each person weaves a garment of 613 threads with his mitzvos, and Klal Yisrael weaves a collective garment since Matan Torah; this generation weaves the last thread, where Moshiach is found. He adds that Krias Shema's last word 'emes' is not written and must be added with force, as emes is hidden in the end of days.

title.en: Vacation, the garment, and daily mussar

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the summer pull of Tammuz and Av, when people on vacation first take off their garments, and recalls that after Adam's sin Hashem gave him garments as protection. Since even the meraglim forgot, he says one needs reminders, and advises learning some mussar every day.

title.en: Hashem loves every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Satan tells a person that Hashem hates him, as the meraglim's generation claimed, and Rashi answers that Hashem loves them. He tells of a chassid who traveled days just to see his Rebbe, who told him his love for his chassidim is nothing compared to Hashem's love for even a moser. He stresses that love is a need like food, for children and even malachim, and that Tisha B'Av's readings open with 'banim'.

title.en: Malachi's message and Shabbos Chazon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Malachi, the last navi, left a message for the whole exile until Eliyahu comes. He then speaks of Shabbos Chazon, when one can see the third Beis HaMikdash, brings gematrios on Parshas Devarim and Tehillim 89, urges preparing well for this Shabbos, and closes with a brachah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, gathers all of Chanukah and all of Klal Yisrael into one, like the thirty-six lights that merge into a single flame, and reveals the hidden light in every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that a gathering of Jews in love repairs the sale of Yosef, and that Chanukah is the aspect of Yosef. In the days of the Nesi'im each tribe had its own day, but Zos Chanukah counts everything together. Every Jew is a letter of the Torah and holds one mitzvah; the thirty-six lights match thirty-six masechtos, and on Zos Chanukah the leftover wicks are burned in one flame. This unity undoes the Greeks, and it rests on bittul before every other Jew. Bending down to light the menorah brings down the thirteen middos of rachamim and the treasure of free gifts. Chanukah comes from the fiftieth gate, the Yovel, like the Exodus; the menorah is a model of the third Beis HaMikdash. The last light is the light of Moshiach. The empty cups of the menorah stand for Jews whose hidden light is not yet lit, and the Mashgiach closes that on Zos Chanukah every simple Jew can achieve what tzaddikim achieve on Yom Kippur.

en: Jews sitting together with love is the repair of the sale of Yosef, and Chanukah is the aspect of Yosef.
In the twelve days of the Nesi'im each tribe had its own festival, but on Zos Chanukah everything is counted together as one.
The thirty-six lights correspond to the thirty-six masechtos, and on Zos Chanukah all the wicks are burned together in one great flame.
The heart of Yiddishkeit is to be mevatel oneself before every Jew, because each one has a virtue that one does not have.
Bending down to light the Chanukah lights accustoms a Jew to humility, which brings down the thirteen middos of rachamim and the treasure of free gifts.
The menorah, made by Hashem Himself, is a model of the third Beis HaMikdash and of the fiftieth gate.
The empty cups of a one-piece menorah stand for Jews whose hidden light does not yet shine; Hashem judges them by that hidden light.

title.en: Zos Chanukah counts everything together

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that Jews sitting together in love repair the sale of Yosef, and that Chanukah is the aspect of Yosef. He contrasts the twelve days of the Nesi'im, when each tribe had its own day, with Zos Chanukah, when all the offerings are counted together and there is no more strife between Ephraim and Yehuda.

title.en: Thirty-six lights in one flame

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew holds one mitzvah, that the thirty-six lights match thirty-six masechtos, and that on Zos Chanukah the wicks are burned together in one flame. This unity undoes the Greeks; it rests on bittul before every Jew, and he brings the Divrei Yisrael on Yosef's words to his brothers about different paths.

title.en: Bending down and the treasure of free gifts

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that lighting below ten tefachim trains a Jew to bend down, which is why Al HaNissim is in Modim and why Chanukah brings down the thirteen middos of rachamim. He brings the Midrash of the treasure of free gifts, Yishmael's teshuvah in letting Yitzchak go first, and ties this to Yosef and to the Yovel.

title.en: Mai Chanukah: the light of the Yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara asks 'What is Chanukah?' and answers that Chanukah comes from the fiftieth gate, the Yovel, like the Exodus, which is awakened by questions. The Yovel comes from Hashem alone, not from a person's deeds, so even the lowest Jew will run to Moshiach, and the third Beis HaMikdash will be built by Hashem.

title.en: The menorah and the third Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Moshe found the menorah hard: it was made by Hashem Himself and is a model of the third Beis HaMikdash and of the fiftieth gate, which Moshe did not attain. On Zos Chanukah the last light, matching the last masechta, completes the light of Moshiach and the rebuilding of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Chanukah completes the crown

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the Hallel still to be said and explains that Chanukah, the last mitzvah instituted by the Sages, completes the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, the crown that will be placed on Moshiach. He ties Chanukah to chen, to Yosef's blessing to Binyamin and to Kislev, and says Chanukah's judgment is by the hidden light in every Jew.

title.en: The empty cups of the menorah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the custom is a one-piece menorah with empty cups, when one makes no brachah over empty vessels. He answers that the empty cups are Jews whose hidden light does not yet shine; Hashem sees that they are not empty, and when Moshiach comes all the lights will shine toward the menorah.

title.en: Every simple Jew a tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach repeats the saying of the Ruzhiner that what tzaddikim achieve on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur every simple Jew can achieve on Zos Chanukah, and explains it with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim'. He says every minute of Zos Chanukah is a treasure, and closes with brachos for children, life and sustenance and for the revelation of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: סעודת רשות - היחיד או הרבים? ואודות פרות השמנות הנבלעות בתוך פרות הכחושות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah meal is a 'seudas reshus' in which singing turns the public domain of golus into a private domain of Hashem, and that the lean cows of Pharaoh's dream, which swallowed the fat ones, will in the end have to spit out every holy spark.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that Chanukah carries no obligation of a meal, so its meal is a 'seudas reshus'. Chanukah lights are placed in the public domain below ten tefachim, bringing a private domain of holiness into the public one. 'Reshus' alone lacks a word; by singing praise, as one must at a redemption, a Jew adds 'hayachid', because even in the public domain there is a spark of G-dliness. In Pharaoh's dream, the lean cows stood beside the fat ones, stunned like a person entering Jerusalem, because the sitra achra knows the power of holiness and that it must eventually spit out what it swallowed. From the Midrash on 'ketz sam lachoshech' and Yosef's two extra years in prison he explains how a set time of redemption can be prolonged, calls on each Jew to hasten it, and sees baalei teshuvah as the first drops before the rain.

en: Since Chanukah has no obligatory meal, its meal is a 'seudas reshus', and by singing at it a Jew adds the missing word and makes it a 'reshus hayachid'.
The Chanukah light is placed in the public domain below ten tefachim, bringing a private domain of holiness into the public one.
The lean cows that swallowed the fat ones represent the sitra achra swallowing Jewish souls, but in the end it must spit out everything.
A set time of redemption can be prolonged, as Yosef's release was delayed two years, and each Jew should ask what he does to hasten it.
The teshuvah movement before Moshiach is like the light rain that comes before a heavy rain.

The light is placed in the public domain, and by singing, as one must at a redemption, a Jew reveals the spark of G-dliness there and makes it a 'reshus hayachid'.

title.en: Why the lean cows stood still

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the hungry lean cows of Pharaoh's dream 'stood' beside the fat ones. Comparing them to a person who stops in awe on entering Jerusalem, he explains that the sitra achra knows the power of holiness and that whatever it swallows it must in the end spit out, and more.

title.en: A ketz that was prolonged

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on 'ketz sam lachoshech' and a calculation of the ketz attributed to the Arizal that passed without redemption. He answers from Yosef, who was meant to be in prison ten years but had it extended because he leaned on the butler instead of on Hashem alone.

title.en: Chanukah, time to hasten the ketz

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Chanukah a time of redemption when the hidden light is revealed, and says each Jew should make a reckoning of what he does so the ketz is hastened. From the public domain of golus one makes a private domain by singing zemiros before the redemption, and he closes with a tefilah that Hashem's kingship be revealed.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: A niggun is sung.

title.en: Baalei teshuvah: the light rain before the rain

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the swallowed souls, so hidden they cannot be recognized as Jews, and brings the Gemara that light rain precedes a heavy rain: before Moshiach there are already glimmers of teshuvah. He describes young men he saw who became chassidish and daven with fire, and says that one must keep kindling more lights.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Zos Chanukah all the lights, all the masechtos, all the shevatim and all of Klal Yisroel come together into one great lighting, through which every Jew can reach what a tzaddik reaches on Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's 'pach shel shemen': the jar was nearly empty, yet its last drops burned all eight nights. He brings the Ruzhiner: what a tzaddik achieves on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew achieves on Zos Chanukah, and contrasts the wordless shofar with Chanukah's hallel and thanks. Chanukah is the last mitzvah, completing the crown of mitzvos; its lights match the masechtos, ending with Niddah, galus and Eliyahu. The seudah is a voluntary mitzvah of love that unites Jews, and on Zos Chanukah, like the total of the nesi'im's offerings, everything joins into one. Through the Ramban, the Sfas Emes and a story of Rav Chaim Vital, he shows that Aharon lights with every Jew. He adds that Zos Chanukah is a day of remembering the barren, tells of a ba'al teshuvah's lineage, and closes with the Ruzhiner's word about winning.

en: The Ruzhiner said that what a tzaddik can accomplish on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew can accomplish on Zos Chanukah, because Chanukah reaches down to the lowest levels.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem is served with the wordless breath of the shofar; on Chanukah, when there is already speech, He is served with hallel and thanks.
Chanukah is the last mitzvah given, and with it the crown of the mitzvos is completed.
The Chanukah lights correspond to the masechtos of the Oral Torah; the last, Niddah, matches the final galus and ends with Eliyahu, herald of Moshiach.
On Zos Chanukah all the masechtos, all the shevatim and all the lights join into one, as the Torah totals all the nesi'im's offerings together.
Since the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Menorah, every Jew's home becomes a Beis HaMikdash and Aharon HaKohen comes to light together with him.

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'pach shel shemen' as a nearly empty jar whose last drops burned all eight nights, a light beyond counting, and touches on the Shelah's question why Chanukah is eight days. He then brings the Ruzhiner: what a tzaddik achieves on Rosh Hashanah, a simple Jew achieves on Zos Chanukah.

title.en: Breath, speech, and the last mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Rosh Hashanah, served with the wordless shofar, with Chanukah, served with hallel and thanks. Chanukah is the last mitzvah that completes the crown of mitzvos, and through the Bnei Yissaschar in the name of Rav Pinchas of Koretz its lights match the masechtos, ending with Niddah, galus and Eliyahu.

title.en: A seudah of love that unites

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah seudah is voluntary, a mitzvah Jews take on out of love, like hiddur, and that such a meal brings Jews together. Each Jew has his own light and masechta, and on Zos Chanukah all are thrown into one great fire of achdus.

title.en: Zos Chanukah: everything joins into one

summary.en: Each day of Chanukah is the yom tov of one nasi, but Zos Chanukah belongs to all, as the Torah totals all the offerings. The Mashgiach adds the thirteen middos of rachamim and the Arizal's teaching that each day's mitzvos rise the next morning, tells how the Imrei Emes was aroused by 'kol hakelim', and invites all to daven together with all their kelim.

title.en: Aharon lights with every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that Aharon's consolation hints to the Chanukah lights, and asks what aliyah this is for his tribe if all Jews light. Through the Sfas Emes, that Chanukah is a remembrance of the Menorah, and Rav Chaim Vital's story of Rav Pinchas ben Yair, he explains that Aharon HaKohen enters every Jew who lights.

title.en: The hidden Menorah and remembering the barren

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds the reverse: through the Chiddushei HaRim, quoted by the Sfas Emes, that the hidden Menorah still burns, our lighting kindles Aharon's Menorah. He then brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah, and above all Zos Chanukah, is a time of remembering the barren, and says to pray for Tzion.

title.en: A ba'al teshuvah and his lineage; blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a ba'al teshuvah whose mother traced her lineage and found she descends from Rav Meir of Premishlan, and explains that Chanukah lights are lit outside, to kindle extinguished souls. He ends with blessings and with the eight names of Moshiach in Yeshayahu, which he links to the eight days.

title.en: What is won on Zos Chanukah stays won

summary.en: After an interlude at the seudah, the Mashgiach quotes the Ruzhiner that what is won on Zos Chanukah is not lost, tells of the custom of tzaddikim to drink punch on Zos Chanukah, and closes wishing that Chanukah flow into Purim in Yerushalayim with Moshiach.

catalogTitle: ביכורים - Bringing the Fruit of ראשית to the Place of ראשית

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that bikurim, the first-ripened fruit, is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the place where creation began, and from there he builds a call to rise early in Elul and use the days of teshuvah before Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah of bikurim and the idea that sparks of holiness are hidden in everything a person eats and uses, each one bound to his own nefesh. Through the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'hungry and thirsty' and the gifts of leket, shikchah and pe'ah, he shows that a thing reaches the person whose nature it matches. Rashi describes the fig that ripens first; such an early riser is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the first point of creation, and given to the kohanim, who are zerizim. Rosh Hashanah is the same beginning in time, so in Elul, the tired end of the year, one must wake up. He then lays out four periods of teshuvah, 30, 40, 52 and 122 days, hinted in the pesukim of Vayelech, Nitzavim and Haazinu, and reads the 122 pesukim of Ki Savo as rebuke for a past year whose days were wasted.

en: Every food, garment and possession holds sparks of holiness that belong to one specific person's nefesh, and only he can raise them by using it for Hashem.

Bikurim, the fruit that ripens before all others, is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the first place created, and given to the kohanim, who are zerizim, so that the early riser goes to the place and the people of early rising.

Rosh Hashanah is in time what the Beis HaMikdash is in space, the beginning; therefore Elul, the tired end of the year, is the time to wake up early and prepare, and one does not sleep on Rosh Hashanah.
There are four periods of teshuvah: 30 days to Rosh Hashanah, 40 to Yom Kippur, 52 to Shemini Atzeres according to the Zohar, and 122 to the last day of Chanukah according to the Arizal.
The 122 pesukim of Ki Savo, read before the new year, are rebuke about the past year: its 122 days of teshuvah were not used, and the Mashgiach urges not to repeat that mistake.

title.en: Bikurim and the sparks in everything we use

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of the parsha about bringing the first fruits to the kohen, then introduces the idea that since Adam's sin sparks of holiness are imprisoned in all we eat, wear and live in, each bound to a particular person's nefesh.

title.en: Why people must be hungry and thirsty

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's explanation of 'hungry and thirsty': people must eat so that with their brachos they release the sparks in their food, which are an extension of their own nefesh, and he illustrates it with a shared apple and a lost pen.

title.en: Leket, shikchah and pe'ah fit the poor man

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the gifts the Torah gives the poor carry the poor man's character: leket falls to the ground as he lies in the dust, shikchah is forgotten as he seems forgotten, and pe'ah is at the edge as he lives at the fringe of society.

title.en: The early fig goes to the place of beginning

summary.en: From Rashi's description of the fig that ripens first, the Mashgiach explains that this 'early riser' is brought to the Beis HaMikdash, the even shesiyah from which the world spread out, and given to the kohanim, who are zerizim.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, Elul and not sleeping

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rosh Hashanah is the beginning of time as the Beis HaMikdash is of space, while Elul is the tired end of the year when one must rise early. He brings Tehillim 92 on staying fresh in the house of Hashem, the Shulchan Aruch and the Rambam on not sleeping, and Yaakov's regret at sleeping at the place of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Forty days that decide the year

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Berachos that one may daven for a boy only during the first forty days, and applies it to the year: the thirty days of Elul and ten of Tishrei determine its character, like Moshe Rabbeinu's forty days ending on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Four periods of teshuvah: 30, 40, 52, 122

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out the Gemara on tzaddikim and beinonim, the Zohar's extension to Shemini Atzeres and the Arizal's to the last day of Chanukah, and, counting every month as thirty days, arrives at 30, 40, 52 and 122 days of teshuvah.

title.en: The hint in the parshiyos of teshuvah

summary.en: Seeking the periods of teshuvah in the parshiyos read in that season, the Mashgiach explains why Vezos Habrachah is not counted and matches the pesukim of Vayelech, Nitzavim and Haazinu to the days, totaling 122. He relates that a listener once noted Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim and asks why that repetition is needed.

title.en: Ki Savo as rebuke for the past year

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Ki Savo's 122 pesukim speak of the past year: its days of teshuvah were not used, and he lists the year's suffering and the growing impurity. He then stresses preparing to crown Hashem, who alone decides the fate of nations, whose leaders are puppets in His hands.

title.en: Wake up and use the days

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the image of the sleeping figs, brings the Levi whose clothes were burnt for sleeping in the Beis HaMikdash, and urges using the 30, 40, 52 or 122 days. He tells the listeners that they are facing the Beis HaMikdash, the place from which teshuvah spreads, and closes with a brachah; a short exchange with listeners follows.

catalogTitle: בחינת שמיני עצרת' הקב"ה רוצה להיות אצלינו עוד יום אחד

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Shemini Atzeres, when Jews come up to Hashem and He holds them back one more day, with Zos Chanukah, when Hashem Himself comes down to the lowest Jews to stay with them and light them up.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shemini Atzeres: Sukkos has a reason, but Shemini Atzeres has none except that Hashem wants to be with His children, as a father needs no reason to come to his child's simcha. Chanukah goes further. On Shemini Atzeres the Jews come up to Hashem; on Chanukah Hashem comes down to the extinguished souls in the street, and on Zos Chanukah He says He will stay below with them, like a king who comes to a lowly place because his bride is there. From this the Mashgiach speaks of drawing close the distant Jews. He brings the Targum Yonasan that the korbanos of the twelve nesiim, read on Zos Chanukah, nullify the twelve princes of Yishmael, and tells how Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky explained why religious children honor their parents. He closes that Zos Chanukah sums up all of Chanukah, nullifying Esav and Yishmael, and blesses the listeners with a good year.

en: Shemini Atzeres has no reason of its own; Hashem simply wants to be together with the Jews, as a father comes to his child's simcha without needing a reason.
On Shemini Atzeres the Jews come up to Hashem, while on Chanukah Hashem comes down to the lowest levels, to the extinguished souls in the street, to light them up.
Zos Chanukah is a day for drawing close distant Jews who do not even know Shema Yisroel, and for letting oneself be drawn close.
Following the Targum Yonasan, the korbanos of the twelve nesiim nullify the twelve princes of Yishmael.
Zos Chanukah is the sum of all the days of Chanukah, when one takes stock of what one gained, and it is even greater than Chanukah itself.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the twelve princes of Yishmael and of Esav are leaders of the sitra achra, and the korbanos of the nesiim nullify them. He then says Zos Chanukah sums up the whole Chanukah: one counts what one gained, and the day is greater than Chanukah itself.

title.en: Zos Chanukah against Amalek; a good year

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Zos Chanukah the small, hidden point of holiness in every Jew, the 'pach shemen' that was never defiled, prevails over the great mass of bad, as the few prevailed over the many.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yehuda repeats to Yosef everything both already knew, and answers that he wanted to settle it in his own mind and accept Hashem's guidance in every detail. Every event holds the hidden light of Hashem's will, but the klipah of Yavan covers it; the Chanukah lights reveal it, just as the two words 'Ani Yosef' answered all the brothers' suffering. He brings the Sfas Emes that in these days one must strengthen the small point found in every Jew, the pure flask that keeps its blessing. Chanukah comes from the 'eighth world' above nature, so its miracle followed no rules: the few overcame the many. Zos Chanukah is therefore the final sealing for those whose sins outweigh their merits. He ties this to the ner maaravi, a Ruzhiner story about plain Jews, the Kosel, and 'lo me'astim'.

en: Yehuda repeated what was already known in order to settle it in his own mind and accept Hashem's guidance in every detail.
Hashem's will is hidden in every event as the 'ohr haganuz'; the klipah of Yavan covers it and lighting the Chanukah candles reveals it.
Every Jew has a small point, like the pure flask of oil, which nothing can extinguish and on which blessing rests.
Chanukah comes from the 'eighth world' above nature, so its miracle followed no rules of nature or arithmetic: the few held the many.
Zos Chanukah is the final sealing for those who could not be judged favorably by the count on Rosh Hashanah, because then a small point of mitzvos outweighs many sins.
The ner maaravi and the Kosel Hamaaravi represent the point that is never extinguished, the worth of the plain Jews who sit by the western wall.

title.en: Why Yehuda repeated everything

summary.en: After an opening niggun, the Mashgiach asks why Yehuda retells Yosef all that happened, and answers that he wanted it settled in his mind so as to accept Hashem's guidance in every detail. Nothing happens by chance, but the klipah of Yavan covers this point.

title.en: The hidden light and 'Ani Yosef'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the hidden light of Hashem's will is in every event, and the Chanukah lights reveal it. In the parsha things only get worse for the brothers until two words, 'Ani Yosef', answer everything, as the Midrash says all will be answered when Hashem says 'Ani Hashem'.

title.en: The small point and the eighth world

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sfas Emes that in these days one must strengthen the small point in every Jew, the pure flask that keeps its blessing. Chanukah, from the 'eighth world' above nature, let one night's oil burn eight nights, and like a bris on the eighth day the Jew laughs at nature.

title.en: The few held the many

summary.en: Citing the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains the Chanukah miracle as 'a little holding much', like the Beis Hamikdash courtyard and the victory of the few over the many. In this world bad is the majority, yet Zos Chanukah, with all eight days' wicks burnt together, shows the good prevailing.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as the final sealing

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Sfas Emes on the small point and asks what Zos Chanukah's final sealing adds to Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. Rosh Hashanah judges by count, merits against sins; Zos Chanukah is for those whose sins are many, when a small point of mitzvos outweighs them, as will be revealed in the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Taking Chanukah along; Selach na

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the hidden light to chein and to Aharon, and says one must take the warmth of Chanukah along afterward. He brings the Likutei Moharan that 'selach na' holds the initials of Chanukah, explains why the words about sin are left out, and connects Mattisyahu ben Yochanan to Rosh Hashanah and to grace.

title.en: The ner maaravi and the plain Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the Chanukah miracle to the ner maaravi of Shimon HaTzaddik, a testimony that the Shechinah rests in Israel. He tells how the Ruzhiner refused to come to a shul that would keep out the plain Jews, and explains that the western wall, where plain Jews sit, holds the point that is never extinguished, like the Kosel Hamaaravi.

title.en: 'Lo me'astim' and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's reading of 'lo me'astim' as referring to the days of the Greeks, and says that 'lo me'astim' equals the ner maaravi in gematria. He says a Jew should leave Chanukah taking the hidden light along, and closes with a blessing for a good final sealing.

catalogTitle: ע"י שירות ותשבחות זוכים לאור של חנוכה

oneLiner.en: Through the Chiddushei HaRim, the Mashgiach explains that the light of Chanukah is Aharon's own light still burning, that it demands more than a person's strength, that Hallel and songs of praise make Chanukah a Yom Tov, and that this light must reach those who are far away.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach repeats teachings of the Chiddushei HaRim on Chanukah. Rashi says Aharon was consoled for missing the dedication of the Mishkan with the lighting of the menorah, and the Ramban, puzzled, links it to the Chanukah of the Chashmonaim. The Chiddushei HaRim explains that Aharon's ner hama'aravi was never extinguished and still burns in its hiding place, and the Chanukah lights come from it; this is 'Zos Chanukah'. The mitzvah of Chanukah also demands more than a person's strength, beyond 'with all your means', since the miracle came through mesirus nefesh. The poskim say singing praises turns the Chanukah meal into a seudas mitzvah: the Gemara says the days were fixed as Yom Tov with Hallel and thanksgiving, so the praise itself makes the day a Yom Tov. Finally, Chanukah light must reach those far away, and the Mashgiach calls for supporting kiruv as an opportunity Hashem sends today.

en: The Chanukah lights draw from Aharon's ner hama'aravi, which was never extinguished and still burns where it was hidden.
Other Yamim Tovim bring down the lights of their miracles, but on Chanukah the very same miracle still burns, even physically.
The mitzvah of Chanukah demands more than a person's strength, beyond 'with all your means', since the miracle came through mesirus nefesh.
Saying Hallel and singing praises is what turns Chanukah into a Yom Tov, and so it makes the meal a seudas mitzvah.
The Chanukah light must be brought to those who are 'below ten tefachim', the ones far from Torah.
The unprecedented opportunity for kiruv in this generation is a sign that Hashem is sending the merit of the mitzvah before the ingathering of the exiles.

title.en: Aharon's light still burns

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi and the Ramban on Aharon being consoled with the lighting of the menorah, and the Chiddushei HaRim's explanation that Aharon's ner hama'aravi still burns and the Chanukah lights come from it. This, he says, is why the last day is called 'Zos Chanukah'.

title.en: A mitzvah beyond one's strength

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the usual limit on spending for a mitzvah with Chanukah, where even a poor man must borrow or sell his garment, and explains that a mitzvah above nature demands more than one's strength. He adds the Chiddushei HaRim that the Chanukah light, placed outside, reaches even the one who is outside, and that its rise comes with Hallel the next morning.

title.en: Songs of praise make the seudah a mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the poskim's advice to sing songs of praise turns the Chanukah meal, otherwise optional, into a seudas mitzvah. He answers with the Chiddushei HaRim: the Gemara says the days were fixed as Yom Tov with Hallel and thanksgiving, so the praise creates the Yom Tov, and a Yom Tov calls for a seudah.

title.en: Bringing the light to those far away

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Chanukah light must reach those 'below ten tefachim' and calls on the gathering to support Torah Umesorah's work with baalei teshuvah. He explains that the unprecedented chance for kiruv today is a mitzvah Hashem sends, as He sent the angels to Lot, before the ingathering of the exiles, and ties it to Yosef leaving prison in parshas Mikeitz.

catalogTitle: The 6th Month Corresponds to the 6th אושפיזין - Yosef הצדיק

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Elul, the sixth month, corresponds to Yosef HaTzaddik, the sixth of the ushpizin, who embodies Seder Taharos, so that Elul is the month of purity that prepares for the holiness of Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'lachazos b'noam Hashem', said in Elul, and the bond of 'ani l'dodi v'dodi li'. Following the Arizal, the seven months from Nissan to Tishrei correspond to the seven ushpizin, so Elul is Yosef's month. He then asks why Yaakov taught Yosef only five orders of Mishnah, as the Baal HaTurim reads 'zekunim', and why Yaakov, unlike Avraham, needed teachers at all. He builds an answer from the stages of Klal Yisrael: the avos and the seven ro'im are single trunks, the shevatim are branches. Yosef was a ro'eh, not a shevet, and corresponds to Seder Taharos, which he knew by himself. Avraham, the first, contains all the days. Yosef's purity explains how Yaakov sensed him in the produce from Mitzrayim, his title 'tzaddik', and the special quality of Mishkan Shiloh. Elul, Yosef's taharah, prepares for Rosh Hashanah's kedusha, and the Mashgiach urges using the forty days.

en: Following the Arizal, the seven months from Nissan to Tishrei correspond to the seven ushpizin, so Elul, the sixth month, is the month of Yosef.
The avos and the seven ro'im are single units, trunks of the tree, while the twelve shevatim are branches; Yosef was not a shevet but one of the seven ro'im.
Each of the seven ro'im corresponds to a day of the week and an order of Mishnah, with Yosef, the sixth, corresponding to Seder Taharos.
Yaakov taught Yosef only five orders, as the word 'zekunim' hints, because Yosef knew Seder Taharos by himself.
Yaakov sensed that Yosef was alive in Mitzrayim from the purity, the taste and fragrance, of the produce that Yosef personally handled.
Elul, Yosef's month of taharah, is the preparation for Rosh Hashanah, because purity must come before holiness.

title.en: Elul, the sixth month, and Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'lachazos b'noam Hashem' as a wish that Hashem have nachas from us, and describes Elul as the time of 'ani l'dodi v'dodi li'. He then states that Elul is the sixth month and, following the Arizal, corresponds to Yosef, the sixth of the ushpizin.

title.en: Ben zekunim and the missing Taharos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's two explanations of 'ben zekunim', the second being that Yaakov passed on to Yosef all the Torah he had received. He then brings the Baal HaTurim's hint that 'zekunim' spells five orders of Mishnah, and asks where Seder Taharos is.

title.en: Avraham knew Torah by instinct

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Chazal's statement that Avraham's kidneys taught him Torah: he knew the whole Torah by instinct, as animals know what is in their nature. He asks why Yaakov, the choicest of the avos, needed teachers, and asks too why Yaakov sensed that Yosef was in Mitzrayim only at that point.

title.en: Trunk and branches: avos, shevatim, seven shepherds

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the stages of Klal Yisrael: single avos, then twelve shevatim as branches of Yaakov's trunk, then seventy souls, then a nation. On the three regalim the shevatim return to their trunk, and the seven ro'im, the ushpizin, are units who sustain every Jew; he notes the two orders of the ushpizin.

title.en: Twelve paths and seven: the future elevation

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the twelve paths of Krias Yam Suf with the seven streams of the future split in Yeshaya 11, when the shevatim will be raised to the level of the ro'im and the strife of Ephraim and Yehuda will end. He compares the twelve weekday requests of Shemoneh Esrei to Shabbos's single brachah, and Musaf of Rosh Chodesh to the unity of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Yosef a ro'eh, not a shevet; Chok LeYisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef was one of the seven ro'im, not a shevet, so Ephraim and Menashe took his place; the brothers mistook his higher conduct for arrogance, and Rashi's reading of 'even Yisrael' as father and son shows he had the quality of an av. He then describes the Chok LeYisrael order of the Arizal, matching each day to one of the ro'im and an order of Mishnah.

title.en: The first contains all: why Taharos is missing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham, as the first, 'ba bayamim', comes with all the days, so he knew the whole Torah by himself, while Yitzchak knew only Seder Moed and the shevatim had to be taught everything. This answers the Baal HaTurim's question: Yaakov did not need to teach Yosef Taharos, and he loved him because he had to teach him less.

title.en: Each av and his order of Mishnah

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the correspondences: Avraham is Zeraim and emunah, which is why Zeraim opens with Brachos; Yitzchak is Moed; Yaakov is Nashim, as seen in his toil for his wives; Nezikin, which sharpens the mind, belongs to Moshe; and Kodashim to Aharon.

title.en: Taharah gives taste and fragrance

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David is the hidden 'sod' of Shabbos, and brings the end of Sotah that when taharah was taken away, produce lost its taste and fragrance. Yosef is taharah: produce he handled in Mitzrayim carried a holy fragrance, and from it Yaakov knew that Yosef was alive, uniting Rashi's and Targum Yonasan's readings of 'vayar Yaakov'.

title.en: Yosef the tzaddik and Potiphar's wife

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why only Yosef carries the title 'tzaddik': a seventeen-year-old torn from his father's home, he withstood Potiphar's wife for a whole year. He retells from Chazal her threats and his answers from pesukim, ending with 'Hashem ohev tzaddikim'.

title.en: Mishkan Shiloh, the Mishkan of Yosef

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Mishkan Shiloh, in Yosef's territory, with the Beis HaMikdash in Yerushalayim: Shiloh was temporary, but kodashim could be eaten wherever it could be seen, a merit of Yosef's guarding his eyes. He returns to Elul as the sixth month corresponding to Yosef and Tishrei as the seventh, David and malchus.

title.en: Elul prepares: taharah before kedusha

summary.en: As Friday prepares for Shabbos, Elul prepares for Rosh Hashanah; the Mashgiach brings the Likutei Torah that in Elul the King is in the field and anyone may approach him. Taharah precedes kedusha, and he brings the Gemara on the dudaim, pure young men or baalei teshuvah, and the fragrance of the ketores that was smelled at Shiloh.

title.en: The forty days and closing brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur absorbed the teshuvah of Moshe's last forty days on the mountain, and calls on listeners to use them. The thirty days of Elul are Shiloh and the ten days are Yerushalayim, with Rosh Hashanah as the Beis HaMikdash of time; he closes with a brachah for a good year.

catalogTitle: האש של חנוכה מעורר התפשטות הקדושה ע"י עבודת ה' בהתלהבות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ner Chanukah, unlike the mezuzah, carries the fire of kedushah outward, and that Zos Chanukah should carry that fire of zerizus and hislahavus into the whole year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach contrasts two paired mitzvos. The mezuzah, on the right as one enters, is a guard that keeps the outside forces from coming in; the ner Chanukah, on the left, is for the one going out, so that the kedushah spreads into the public domain. Milah and priah form the same pair. Gehinnom has a fire for sins and snow for mitzvos done coldly, and the eight Chanukah lights, above nature, are the fire of zerizus that answers the snow. On Zos Chanukah he calls for davening tomorrow early and loudly. Like Shemini Atzeres for Sukkos, the eighth day is hard to leave and carries the fire into the year; chinuch means constant renewal, and the kedushah left after Chanukah is greater than after Sukkos. Hallel and hoda'ah, not the lights, are what remain fixed, and they should be said with fire, together with friends.

en: The mezuzah guards the home from outside forces, while the ner Chanukah brings the kedushah out to the public domain.
The snow of Gehinnom is for mitzvos done coldly, without hislahavus, and the fire of Chanukah is the fire of zerizus that counters it.
Milah and priah are a pair like mezuzah and ner Chanukah: one guards, the other reveals the glory of Hashem.
Like Shemini Atzeres for Sukkos, the eighth day of Chanukah is above time and carries the fire of Chanukah into the whole year.
What stays fixed after Chanukah is Hallel and hoda'ah, and they should continue all year with fire.

summary.en: The opening of the shiur.

title.en: Mezuzah guards, ner Chanukah goes out

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mezuzah is a guard at the door so outside forces do not enter, while the ner Chanukah lets the inner kedushah break out into the public domain. That is why the mezuzah is on the right of one entering and the ner Chanukah on the right of one leaving; they are one of several paired mitzvos.

title.en: Fire and snow; milah and priah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Gehinnom is half fire, for sins of desire, and half snow, for mitzvos done coldly without hislahavus. He then explains that a lo sa'aseh is a guard while a mitzvas aseh spreads the glory of Hashem, and that milah, removing the orlah, is like the mezuzah, while priah, which reveals, is like the ner Chanukah.

title.en: Eight lights, the fire of zerizus

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the ner Chanukah is the fire of zerizus that publicizes the mitzvos outward and burns away the fire of sin. The eight lights lift a Jew above nature, and on Zos Chanukah this fire stands against the snow of Gehinnom.

title.en: Davening tomorrow with fire

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that eight is above nature, as the eighth pasuk of a mizmor turns from nature to the Torah, and appeals to come early tomorrow to say Hallel and Pesukei d'Zimra loudly. He answers someone who asked why they shout in davening: it is not planned, it shouts by itself, as at Neilah.

title.en: Zos Chanukah as Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Chanukah completes Sukkos: seven days with an eighth, which is like Shemini Atzeres, a day of 'it is hard for Me to part from you'. Shemini Atzeres has no special mitzvah, only the wish to stay with the Ribono shel Olam, and it carries the sukkah into the year; Zos Chanukah carries the fire of Chanukah the same way.

title.en: Above time: chinuch as renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the eighth is above time and stretches over the whole year, as the Torah reading of the dedication of the mizbe'ach continues 'after it was anointed'. Chinuch means renewal, a gate opened must not be let close, the light must never go out, and the kedushah left after Chanukah, as its leftovers must be burned separately, is greater than after Sukkos.

title.en: Hallel and hoda'ah remain; brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Beraisa and Al Hanisim fix Chanukah with Hallel and hoda'ah and do not mention the lights, and answers that the lights end but Hallel and hoda'ah must remain all year. Hallel lends its kedushah to all of Shacharis and should be said with fire, among friends, as the angels sing together in love; he brings the Radbaz on davening with friends and closes with brachos.

title.en: Closing

summary.en: The close of the shiur, with niggunim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Zos Chanukah as the 'mitzvah tantz' that seals the whole of Chanukah and carries its impression into the entire year, and calls for prayer for Klal Yisrael during the war in Eretz Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach brings the Lechovitcher's teaching that a great wedding runs from the fifteenth of Kislev to Zos Chanukah, its mitzvah tantz. Just as the mitzvah tantz leaves its mark on the chassan and kallah for life, Zos Chanukah carries Chanukah into the whole year; even a small act, like washing negel vasser, can leave an impression for generations. On Zos Chanukah all the nesi'im are read together, and in Al Hanisim one thanks Hashem for the wars. Turning to the war then in Eretz Yisroel, he says the hanhagah of Klal Yisrael is above calculation, so the commentators' predictions mean nothing, and Jews must pray that no Jew be harmed, since before Hashem a single Jew is a 'rov'. The Chashmonaim fought for Hashem's sake, and Hashem made the miracles for the Jews' sake. He closes with the Lechovitcher's words on money given at the mitzvah tantz and Chanukah gelt.

en: Following the Lechovitcher, Zos Chanukah is the mitzvah tantz of the 'wedding' that runs from the fifteenth of Kislev through Chanukah.
As the mitzvah tantz leaves an impression on the chassan and kallah for life, one takes Zos Chanukah along into the whole year and for generations.
Even a small act, such as washing negel vasser one morning, can leave an impression on one's descendants.
The hanhagah of Klal Yisrael is above natural calculation, so the predictions of politicians and military commentators about the war mean nothing.
Zos Chanukah is the time to pray for Klal Yisrael, that not even a single Jew be harmed.
The Chashmonaim went to war for Hashem's sake, and Hashem made the miracles for the sake of the Jews, to show His love for them.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that what happens to Klal Yisrael is guided above any calculation, so one can only pray for a good surprise and a great yeshuah. Zos Chanukah, the culmination of all the miracles, obliges every year to pray for Klal Yisrael, that no Jew be harmed.

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that before Hashem a single Jew counts as a 'rov', and asks to pray that the wars bring true yeshuos. The Chashmonaim fought with mesirus nefesh for Hashem's sake, and Hashem made the miracles for the Jews' sake; he prays that this Chanukah's gift be the coming of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: חיבת הקב”ה לנו במראות הלילה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah, which opens the dark month of Teves, shows Jews Hashem's love, just as Hashem spoke to Yaakov with love 'in the visions of the night' as he went down to Mitzrayim, and that this light must be taken along into Teves.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the sefarim's teaching that Teves is a hard month, the time of the longest night, of darkness and hester panim, and that Chanukah stands at its head to crush the head of the wicked and sweeten the judgments so that Jews can pass through it. He connects this to Parshas Vayigash: Yaakov, about to go down to the exile of Mitzrayim, the darkness of place as Teves is the darkness of time, is told by Hashem 'in the visions of the night' not to fear, for Hashem goes down with him. Chanukah, which the Rambam calls a beloved mitzvah, is a sign of Hashem's love, like the double 'Yaakov, Yaakov' and 'Avraham, Avraham' at the akeidah. A Jew must carry this love and light into Teves, strengthen himself in Torah and tefillah, use the last hours of Zos Chanukah with simple emunah, as the Ruzhiner taught, and bring the Gemara, siddur and Tehillim with him through the dark period until Moshiach.

en: Teves is a hard month of long nights and hester panim, and Chanukah at its head cuts off the head of its darkness and sweetens the judgments so Jews can pass through it.
Mitzrayim is the darkness of place as Teves is the darkness of time, and Yaakov going down there was told by Hashem 'in the visions of the night' not to fear.
Chanukah is a beloved mitzvah through which Hashem shows the Jews that He loves them.
A Jew must take the light and love of Chanukah with him into Teves and strengthen himself in Torah and tefillah.
The light of Zos Chanukah is the greatest light, the eight that is above nature, and it leads into the heart of Teves.
Teves is a time ruled by the 'dogs', and one passes through it by taking along the Chanukah light, the Gemara, the siddur and Tehillim until Moshiach.

title.en: Yaakov's descent: 'do not fear'

summary.en: From Parshas Vayigash the Mashgiach shows Yaakov going down to Mitzrayim, the darkness of place as Teves is the darkness of time, and Hashem telling him in the visions of the night not to fear because He goes down with him; a Jew with emunah draws strength from this.

title.en: A beloved mitzvah: 'Yaakov, Yaakov'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Chanukah is a beloved mitzvah, a sign that Hashem loves the Jews, and compares it to the double 'Yaakov, Yaakov' before the descent to Mitzrayim and 'Avraham, Avraham' after the akeidah, both expressions of love.

title.en: Taking the light of Zos Chanukah along

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew must take the love shown in the visions of the night into Teves and strengthen himself in Torah and tefillah; Zos Chanukah is the greatest light, and he asks that tomorrow's Hallel, the last of Chanukah, light up these hard times.

title.en: Through Teves with simple emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ruzhiner's saying that a simple Jew can accomplish with his tefillos on Zos Chanukah what a great tzaddik accomplishes on Rosh Hashanah, mentions the sefarim on Teves as the rule of the 'dogs' and a story from the Bnei Yissaschar, and closes that one passes through Teves by taking along Chanukah, the Gemara, the siddur and Tehillim until Moshiach.

catalogTitle: The Current פרשיות Allude to the גמר החתימה (Explanation of the Concept of פקידה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the sedros read in the season of teshuvah hint at the four periods of judgment, from Rosh Hashanah until Zos Chanukah, and calls on his listeners to build protection for Klal Yisrael in a coming year of pekidah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach lists four judgment periods from Rosh Chodesh Elul: 30 days to Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, 40 to Yom Kippur for beinonim, 52 to Shemini Atzeres, and 122 to Zos Chanukah. Nitzavim (40 pesukim), Vayeilech (30) and Haazinu (52) hint at them, and together they make 122, as does Ki Savo. He explains that Ki Savo reproaches the wasted 122 days of last year, while the coming 122 are only hinted, out of respect for Klal Yisrael. As a sample, he finds both orders of the ushpizin in Haazinu's 48th and 50th pesukim. He then contrasts Sukkos, holy like the Beis HaMikdash and above ten tefachim, with Chanukah, below ten. Turning to the coming year, Tav Shin Samach, a year of pekidah, he explains why such years were often tragic, points to hopeful signs, and urges teshuvah and Torah as Klal Yisrael's true protection.

en: There are four periods of judgment counted from Rosh Chodesh Elul: 30 days to Rosh Hashanah, 40 to Yom Kippur, 52 to Shemini Atzeres and 122 to Zos Chanukah.
The pesukim of Nitzavim (40), Vayeilech (30) and Haazinu (52) match these periods, and together they make 122.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim reproach last year's unused 122 days, while the coming 122 days are hinted only through a combination of sedros, out of respect for Klal Yisrael.
The sukkah carries the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash and stays above ten tefachim, while Chanukah is its opposite: below ten, in the public domain, in the dark nights of Teves.
The coming year, Tav Shin Samach, is a year of pekidah, yet nobody knows when Moshiach will come, and such years were often tragic because the Satan accuses.
Each Yom Tov gives a gift for the year, and Sukkos gives protection; those who learn Torah and do teshuvah must supply that protection for Klal Yisrael.
