title.en: Four periods of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out four periods for teshuvah counted from Rosh Chodesh Elul: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Shemini Atzeres according to the Zohar, and Zos Chanukah according to the Bas Ayin. He counts 122 days to Zos Chanukah, taking Cheshvan as 30 days.

title.en: Nitzavim, Vayeilech and Haazinu count the days

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Vayeilech's 30 pesukim, Nitzavim's 40 and Haazinu's 52 match the periods, explains why Nitzavim comes first, and excludes Vezos Habrachah. Together they make 122, and his son-in-law added that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim.

title.en: Ki Savo: last year's 122 days

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the 122 is hinted twice and why it is not stated in one sedra. He answers that Ki Savo, the sedra of the curses that ends the old year, reproaches the 122 days of last year that were not used, and calls to use the coming days for teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: Why the coming 122 days are only hinted

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three sedros state 30, 40 and 52 clearly, but the 122 days ahead are only hinted, because needing so long is a disgrace, just as Rashi says Moshe gave his rebuke by hint out of respect for Klal Yisrael. He adds that he found hints for many single days in single pesukim.

title.en: The ushpizin in Haazinu's pesukim

summary.en: As a sample, the Mashgiach brings the two orders of the ushpizin in the Zohar, by middos and by chronology, followed by Chassidim and Ashkenazim. He shows that the 48th pasuk of Haazinu names Moshe and hints at Yosef as 'etzem', and the 50th names Aharon and hints at Yosef, so both orders have their hint.

title.en: Sukkah above ten, Chanukah below ten

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Sukkos and Chanukah: a sukkah must be ten tefachim high, learned in the Gemara from the kapores and the rule that the Shechinah never descended below ten, while the Chanukah light belongs below ten. Though the conclusion is a halachah l'Moshe miSinai, he explains that even the Gemara's first thought is Torah and shows a bond between the sukkah and the Kodesh HaKodashim.

title.en: The sukkah as the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Sukkos the high point of Tishrei and Shemini Atzeres its peak, citing the Chasam Sofer. The sefarim say the sukkah has the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash, so one should keep it holy, yet as 'the heavenly mother' it takes a person in whatever state he is; on Shemini Atzeres the sukkah comes into the house.

title.en: Chanukah in the realm of darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is the opposite of the sukkah: its mitzvah is in the public domain, below ten tefachim, on the left side of the door, in the long nights of Teves, the domain of the sitra achra. He reads 'Haazinu hashamayim' as the holy days up to Sukkos and 'v'sishma ha'aretz' as Chanukah, when the Shechinah comes down to the earth.

title.en: Sukkos gives protection; the year Tav Shin Samach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each Yom Tov is a reservoir for the year: Pesach gives geulah, Shavuos Torah, and Sukkos protection, as in 'ufros aleinu sukkas shlomecha'. He then turns to the much-discussed coming year, Tav Shin Samach, stressing that nobody knows when Moshiach will come.

title.en: Pekidah, and nobody knows the end

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains pekidah: years in which Hashem considers bringing Moshiach, which can be found from pesukim and Gemara, yet they are not certainly the year. He brings that Yaakov could not reveal the end, a year in the Gemara that passed, the Rambam's signs of Moshiach, and the story of Bar Koziva whom Rabbi Akiva thought was Moshiach.

title.en: Why years of pekidah were tragic, and signs of hope

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that years of pekidah were often tragic because the Satan, fearing Moshiach, accuses Klal Yisrael, and gives examples: Tav Ches with the decrees of Chmielnicki, the Malbim's year 1914, and Tav Shin. From the words of Manoach's wife he argues that the great things happening now, Jews gathered in Eretz Yisrael and learning Torah, show Hashem's favor and a beginning of the ingathering.

title.en: The true defenders of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the coming year needs protection, and Hashem expects it from those who learn Torah and do mitzvos: teshuvah builds the sukkah, they are the true defense force, and the four minim, the letters of Hashem's Name, are their weapons. He urges trying again for Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos, and closes with a blessing for a year of teshuvah, simchah and geulah.

catalogTitle: מעלת החתימה של זאת חנוכה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Zos Chanukah, the eighth day, belongs to a world above measure, and is a later time of sealing in which Hashem judges even the Jews who remained outside by their hidden inner light.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens the meal of Zos Chanukah by explaining that because Chanukah was established for praise and thanksgiving, singing praises makes its meal a seudas mitzvah. He then asks why the Chashmonaim, who were holy, took kingship, and answers that, like Moshe Rabbeinu, they rose through extraordinary mesirus nefesh to the 'eighth world' above measure, where one person can be both king and kohen. He shows the same idea in the Masorah's counting of words in Mikeitz. Through the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel and the two orders of the tribes, he explains why for Beis Hillel the last day, falling in Teves, is the main day. Zos Chanukah is a later sealing after Yom Kippur, for later generations who did not finish their teshuvah. On that day the Shechina descends to the Jews outside and judges each by the hidden light within him, as a story of the Lubliner shows.

en: Since Chanukah was established for hallel and thanksgiving, singing praises at its meal makes it a seudas mitzvah.
In the 'eighth world', above time, place and measure, one person can be king, kohen and navi together, as Moshe Rabbeinu was and as the Chashmonaim were permitted to be.
For Beis Hillel the main day of Chanukah is the last, when eight lights are lit, and it falls in Teves; for Beis Shammai it is the first day, in Kislev.
Zos Chanukah is a later time of sealing, after Yom Kippur and Hoshana Rabbah, for Jews who did teshuvah but did not complete it.
On Zos Chanukah the Shechina descends to the lowly Jews who stayed outside, and judges each by his hidden or haganuz rather than by his outward deeds.

sealing of judgment after Yom Kippur

title.en: Opening, and singing that makes a seudas mitzvah

summary.en: After opening words about the month of Teves, the long exile and a call for all Jews to be united, the Mashgiach brings the Magen Avraham that singing praises turns the Chanukah meal into a seudas mitzvah, since Chanukah was established for hallel and thanksgiving.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: Interlude.

title.en: Why the Chashmonaim could be kings

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that the Chashmonaim were punished for taking the kingship from Yehudah, and the parsha of the king followed by the kohanim's portion. He asks how Moshe Rabbeinu was king, navi and kohen, and answers that he belonged to the eighth world above measure; the first Chashmonaim rose there through extraordinary mesirus nefesh, so they alone could be both kohen and king.

title.en: Mikeitz: counting words, not verses

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Masorah counts the words of Parshas Mikeitz, unlike every other parsha where it counts verses. He explains that a verse joins words into a thought, while a word joins letters, which are above comprehension and through which the world was created; Mikeitz, read on Chanukah, belongs to that higher level.

title.en: Beis Shammai, Beis Hillel and the last mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the eight lights show the miracle came from the eighth world, and presents the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel: Beis Shammai belongs to the world of tikkun, while in a world still struggling with the yetzer hara the halachah follows Beis Hillel. He adds that Chanukah is the last yom tov and the last rabbinic mitzvah, and that the Torah has two orders of the tribes, the banners and the stones of the choshen.

title.en: Binyamin or Dan: who is last

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the order of the banners, headed by Yehudah and fitting this world after the sin, with the stones on the kohen gadol's choshen. For Beis Shammai the last mitzvah belongs to Binyamin, the last stone, in whose portion the Beis Hamikdash stood; for Beis Hillel the last is the camp of Dan, which Rashi calls the gatherer of all the camps, who returned what the other tribes lost.

title.en: A later sealing after Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that for Beis Shammai the main day falls in Kislev, while for Beis Hillel, as the halachah follows, it falls in Teves. Beis Shammai's view matches the plain Torah she'be'al peh, where Yom Kippur is the final sealing; for Beis Hillel there is a later tikkun, Hoshana Rabbah and Zos Chanukah, revealed in later generations through the Zohar and the Arizal for Jews who did not finish their teshuvah.

title.en: Judged by the hidden light

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Zos Chanukah the Shechina descends to the lowly Jews who stayed outside, hinted in the week's parsha by 'Yaakov Yaakov', an expression of affection as Yaakov went down to Mitzrayim. Every Jew is judged by his hidden inner point, not by his outward sins, and he tells of a kvitel about an informer given to the Lubliner while the man was lighting Chanukah lights.

title.en: The eighth day holds everything

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on each day of Chanukah one nasi brought his offering for the dedication of the altar, but the eighth day includes several nesi'im and all the middos, because above measure the little holds the much. He closes with a prayer that Hashem see the inner light of every Jew in the time before Moshiach and help all Jews together.

catalogTitle: גודל קדושת יוסף - שהיה נרגש במעשי ידיו ריח של קדושה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef stood above the Shevatim as one of the seven 'shepherds', that his sphere was taharah, and that his purity gave the grain he sold in Egypt a taste and smell of kedushah, from which Yaakov knew he was alive.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Shovavim, the six weeks after Sefer Bereishis ends with Yosef's passing, as the time to draw down Yosef's kedushah. He asks why Yaakov loved Yosef for teaching him the Torah of Shem and Ever, and why Yaakov needed a teacher when Avraham grasped the whole Torah alone. He answers with the seven 'shepherds' (the ushpizin), each tied to a day, a middah and a seder of Mishnah: Avraham, the first, includes all, so he needed no teacher; each other shepherd grasped his own seder. Yosef, sixth, is Taharos, so Yaakov taught him only five sedarim, which showed he stood above the Shevatim. Through 'the power of the maker is in the made', Yosef's taharah gave the grain he sold a good taste and smell, from which Yaakov sensed he lived. The Mashgiach turns to today's severe trials, calls for purity, Torah and tefillah, and closes with Hashem's love for those who withstand them.

en: Shovavim follows the end of Sefer Bereishis with Yosef's passing, and its six weeks are meant to draw down Yosef's kedushah of taharah.
Each of the seven shepherds corresponds to a day of the week, a middah and a seder of Mishnah, and grasped his own seder of the Torah without a teacher.
Avraham, the first of the shepherds, includes all of them, which is why he grasped the entire Torah himself and needed no teacher.
Yosef is a shepherd and not one of the Shevatim; his seder is Taharos, so Yaakov had to teach him only five sedarim, and this is why he loved him most.
Because the power of the maker enters what he makes, Yosef's purity put a good taste and smell into the grain he sold, and Yaakov sensed from it that Yosef was alive.
The Mashgiach says today's world is one great Mitzrayim with unprecedented trials, and a Jew must know he is Hashem's emissary to stand firm in it.

title.en: Shovavim and the kedushah of Yosef

summary.en: After thanking the Rosh Yeshivah, the Mashgiach notes that Sefer Bereishis contains two beginnings, the world and Avraham, and that Shovavim follows its end to rectify the point of Avraham's bris. He describes how Yosef brought kedushah into the depraved land of Egypt so that the Jews there stayed holy.

title.en: Two readings of Rashi and 'ben zekunim'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's two readings of 'Yaakov saw that there was grain in Egypt' and says they must be connected. He then brings 'ben zekunim': Yaakov loved Yosef because he passed to him the Torah of Shem and Ever, and the Baal HaTurim reads the word as initials of the sedarim of Mishnah, and asks what then of the other sons, noting that Avraham grasped the whole Torah alone.

title.en: The seven shepherds above the Shevatim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov, the choicest of the Avos, needed to receive the Torah while Avraham did not. He sets out the three levels of Avos, seven shepherds and Shevatim, each shepherd giving all of Klal Yisrael a path in serving Hashem, and shows from Rashi on 'even Yisrael' that Yosef, a son with the level of a father, stood above the Shevatim.

title.en: Days, middos and the sedarim of Mishnah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the order of Chok LeYisrael, which ties each day of the week to a middah and a seder of Mishnah and Gemara. From this he concludes that each shepherd, aligned with one seder, grasped that seder himself without a teacher, as all will in the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Avraham includes all; Yosef is Taharos

summary.en: From the Zohar on the ushpizin and the rule that a first letter includes the whole word, the Mashgiach explains that Avraham, the first shepherd, includes all seven and so needed no teacher, while Yaakov had to receive the other sedarim. Yosef, the sixth, is Taharos, so Yaakov taught him only five sedarim; this explains the Baal HaTurim and why Yaakov loved him above his brothers.

title.en: Emunah, taharah and the taste of fruit

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the six sedarim are hinted in a passuk beginning with 'emunah', and says Avraham's emunah includes the whole Torah. He then explains that taharah, Yosef's quality and the preparation for Shabbos, was a great level in Bayis times, and that since taharah ceased the taste and smell of fruit departed.

title.en: Why Yosef himself sold the grain

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the ruler of Egypt personally sold grain, like a president working in a fruit store. Beyond the simple answer that he wanted to meet his brothers, he explains through 'the power of the maker is in the made' that Yosef's taharah entered the grain, and that Yaakov, tasting and smelling kedushah in it, knew Yosef was alive, which ties Rashi's two readings together.

title.en: The Yishmaelim's spices and Yosef's fragrance

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Arabia took most of the world's immorality and Rashi's chiddush that the Yishmaelim who carried Yosef bore fragrant spices instead of foul-smelling goods. Following Rav Tzadok, he explains that nations clothe a bad trait in an outer show, but Yosef's taharah brought a good smell, and he brings the Gemara that bachurim who never tasted sin will give off a fragrance like Levanon. He concludes that Shovavim is for taking taharah from Yosef.

title.en: Shovavim of old; purity and the taste of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Satmar Rav speaking during Shovavim in Williamsburg over sixty years ago, with the beis medrash packed and no dry eye. He says that in our situation every young man must know this time is set aside for taharah, and that only one who is pure can feel kedushah and taste in Shabbos, tefillah and Torah, in contrast to bachurim who complain that Shabbos bores them.

title.en: Today's trials and our mission

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the moral world of earlier years with today's open street and the new devices that bring the yetzer hara into Jewish homes. He says these are the trials of ikvesa d'Meshicha described at the end of Sotah, that Hashem sends no trial one cannot pass, and that in this world, one great Mitzrayim, a Jew is Hashem's emissary to stay strong in Torah, tefillah and kedushah.

title.en: Precious to Hashem: 'Yaakov, Yaakov'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Chaim Vital's account that the Arizal told him a person of this late generation is very great, and says every act of holding back is precious to Hashem. From 'Yaakov, Yaakov', a term of love said as Yaakov went down to Egypt, he says Hashem loves the bachur who keeps himself pure there; Sefer Bereishis ends with Yosef's passing, one must strengthen oneself, and the tikkun is immersing in learning. He closes with a brachah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: ישראל נקראים על שם השבעה פירות שנשתבחו בהן א"י (שייכות לפרשת ליתרו)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven species are ranked by their closeness to the word 'Eretz', which alludes to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim, and that every Jew, even the lowest, is one of these fruits and is bound to Eretz like the pomegranate.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shir Hashirim's 'your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates', which Rashi applies to the smallest Jews, and with the year's division into four quarters, where Teves and Shevat, like Tammuz and Av, belong to the low last quarter until Tu B'Shvat. He brings the Midrash that the spies were told to take pomegranates and the Gemara in Berachos that the order of blessings follows closeness to the word 'Eretz'. Eretz, he explains, alludes to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim, which is why Moshe repeats it in Devarim. The pomegranate is farthest from Eretz, yet still bound to it. He applies this to Acher and Rabbi Meir, to the dispute of Rav Hamnuna and Rav Chisda, to hair covering and Kimchis, and to the duty to raise up the distant. He closes that every Jew is one of the fruits, and with tefillos for Tu B'Shvat.

en: The importance of each of the seven species follows how close it stands to the word 'Eretz' in the passuk, since Eretz alludes to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim.
Eretz Yisrael corresponds to Olam Haba, so going there, supporting it, eating its fruits and even speaking of it awaken yiras shamayim; for this Moshe repeats the word Eretz throughout Devarim.
The pomegranate is the farthest of the species from Eretz, yet it is still bound to it; so too the lowest Jews, and the low months of the year, remain bound to yiras shamayim.
Teves and Shevat, like Tammuz and Av, are the last and lowest quarter of the year, but from the fifteenth of the month the second half is already taken back into holiness.
Every Jew can identify with one of the seven fruits, and the Torah teaches that the distant one, the pomegranate, must be brought closer and raised up.

candidateTopics: months of the year and their quarters

title.en: Shabbos, Matan Torah and an orchard of pomegranates

summary.en: After brief opening words linking the week's reading of Matan Torah to Shabbos, the Mashgiach brings the passuk 'your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates'. With Rashi he reads it as a dry field that must be watered, and as the smallest Jews, who are full of good deeds like a pomegranate.

title.en: The four quarters of the year and its last part

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the year, like the twelve tribes in their four camps and the letters of the Torah, divides into four parts, the last being like the camp of Dan. Whether one counts from Tishrei or Nissan, Tammuz-Av or Teves-Shevat form the low last quarter, yet Elul and Adar, and the second halves of Av and Shevat, are taken back into holiness. He links the last letters of the Torah to the last generations before Moshiach.

title.en: 'Take of the fruit of the land': the pomegranates

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Moshe told the spies to take pomegranates, notes that 'ha'aretz' and 'rimon' share a gematria, and stresses that a gematria must fit the inner content of the matter. He then brings the Gemara in Berachos that the order of blessings follows the species' closeness to the word 'Eretz', so dates come before pomegranates, and asks what lies in that word.

title.en: Eretz alludes to Olam Haba

summary.en: Asking why the word Eretz appears in almost every chapter of Devarim, the Mashgiach explains that Eretz alludes to Olam Haba, as the Mishnah reads 'they will inherit the land', and that Eretz Yisrael below corresponds to it. Therefore going to Eretz Yisrael, supporting it, eating its fruits and even speaking of it bring yiras shamayim, and Moshe repeated the word to awaken it.

title.en: The name Yisrael and the ranking of the fruits

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that speaking of tzaddikim also brings yiras shamayim, and reads 'Shema Yisrael... a land flowing with milk and honey' as Moshe's wish that the very name of a Jew should arouse it like the name Eretz. The seven species draw from Eretz Yisrael, so each one's rank follows its closeness to the word Eretz: the pomegranate, fifth after the first Eretz, is the farthest.

title.en: The shiurim learned from the seven species

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the whole passuk of the seven species was said for measures of halacha, and goes through them. Each species gives a positive measure the Torah speaks of, except the pomegranate, which marks the point at which a vessel is no longer a vessel; it speaks of what lies outside the Torah's measures.

title.en: The spies in the low months, and Moshe's advice

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the spies went in Tammuz and Av, the pomegranate of the year, felt a fall and lost their desire for Torah and avodah, while the Chiddushei HaRim teaches one must serve Hashem in light and in darkness. Moshe's instruction to take pomegranates was strength for such a time: even the farthest is bound to Eretz, and by binding oneself to yiras shamayim, ehrliche Yidden and Olam Haba one passes through hard times.

title.en: Acher, Rabbi Meir: date or pomegranate

summary.en: Returning to 'your shoots', the Mashgiach says the lowest Jews are like pomegranates. He brings the Gemara in Chagigah: Rabbi Meir learned from Acher, explained as eating a date and throwing away the pit, yet Heaven did not quote him; when Rabbah bar Shila compared it to a pomegranate, eating the inside and throwing away the peel, it was accepted. The Mashgiach asks why, and gives a first answer: a date's waste is inside, a pomegranate's is outside.

title.en: Rav Hamnuna and Rav Chisda: what 'Eretz' means

summary.en: The Mashgiach offers his own answer through the Gemara in Berachos: Rav Hamnuna blessed on dates before pomegranates, saying the date is second to Eretz and the pomegranate fifth. He explains the dispute by the difference between 'a cup of wine' and 'a cup of gold': for Rav Chisda Eretz is only the place where the fruit grows, so the order of the passuk decides; for Rav Hamnuna the fruits are bound to the essence of Eretz, so closeness to the word decides.

title.en: Why Rabbah bar Shila's answer was accepted

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the dispute: if Acher is hinted in a fruit at all, it is the last one. By the view that the last is the date, which has no bond to Eretz, Torah learned from Acher has no bond to Olam Haba and Heaven did not say it; Rabbah bar Shila held that the last is the pomegranate, bound to Eretz, so even Rabbi Meir's Torah from Acher comes from Olam Haba and was accepted. He connects this to 'even the empty ones among you are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate'.

title.en: Hair covering, the pomegranate and Kimchis

summary.en: The Mashgiach discusses the Rashba's view, brought in the Shulchan Aruch's commentaries, about hair that slips out of the braid, against the Zohar's demand to cover every hair. Such hair is like the pomegranate, last yet bound to Eretz; women who cover all their hair are like the date; and Kimchis, whose walls never saw her hair, is like wheat, first after the first Eretz. He asks why the Gemara mentions that she was a seller of flour.

title.en: Why Eretz twice, and raising up the pomegranate

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah writes Eretz twice rather than listing the fruits in order. He answers that writing it once would let one think Eretz is only a vessel for the fruits; writing it twice shows that all the fruits, and so all Jews, are bound to Eretz and Olam Haba. The Torah also places the pomegranate before the date and honey, to teach that the distant one must be brought close and lifted up, as the word 'rimon' suggests.

title.en: Every Jew is one of the fruits; Tu B'Shvat

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Jews are compared to each of the seven species and that every Jew belongs to one of them. On Tu B'Shvat, when one makes a blessing over fruits as the Magen Avraham brings, Hashem as it were makes a blessing over the Jews and rejoices with them; he speaks of the golden fruits Shlomo planted in the Beis Hamikdash, and closes with tefillos for a fine esrog and for good, golden fruits.

catalogTitle: Do Teshuvah!! Create a Year of ישועות for כלל ישראל!

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the 122 pesukim of Ki Savo point to last year's wasted 122 days of teshuvah, while the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu hold out a new chance, and he ties the coming year to the fall of Yishmael and the coming of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Ki Savo is read before Rosh Hashanah so the year ends with its curses. He then lays out four stages of judgment: tzaddikim are sealed on Rosh Hashanah, beinonim on Yom Kippur, others wait until Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeres, and the last until Zos Chanukah. These are hinted in the pesukim: Nitzavim has 40, Vayelech 30 and Haazinu 52, together 122, the number of days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah. Since Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim, he explains that it speaks of last year's 122 days, which were wasted, and the tragedies of the past year followed. The new 122 pesukim bring hope if the period is used. He explains why the threat of Yishmael is so sharp before Moshiach, using the Ba'al HaTurim, and shows that the Rosh Hashanah tefillos and kriah ask for Moshiach and the banishment of Yishmael.

en: There are four stages of judgment for teshuvah: Rosh Hashanah for tzaddikim, Yom Kippur for beinonim, Hoshana Rabbah to Shemini Atzeres, and Zos Chanukah.
Nitzavim's 40, Vayelech's 30 and Haazinu's 52 pesukim match the stages, and together make 122, the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim refer to last year's 122 days of teshuvah, which were wasted, and the troubles of the past year are the result.
The threat of Yishmael is sharpest now because the Satan, knowing that the fall of Yishmael brings his own end and the end of the galus, fights hardest just before Moshiach.
The tefillos and kriah of Rosh Hashanah center on Moshiach, the return of Tziyon's children, and the banishment of Yishmael from Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: Four stages of the sealing of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Ki Savo is read before Rosh Hashanah to end the year with its curses, then explains that tzaddikim are sealed on Rosh Hashanah, beinonim on Yom Kippur, others at Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeres, and the last on Zos Chanukah.

title.en: 122 days hinted in three sedros

summary.en: The Mashgiach finds the four periods in the pesukim of the sedros of the season: Nitzavim's 40 for Elul and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, Vayelech's 30 for the tzaddikim, Haazinu's 52 until Shemini Atzeres, and all three together, 122, until Zos Chanukah.

title.en: Ki Savo: last year's wasted 122 days

summary.en: Asking why Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim, the Mashgiach says it refers to last year's 122 days of teshuvah, which were wasted, and lists the tragedies of the past year as the result. The new 122 pesukim bring hope, and he urges using this period fully.

title.en: The fall of Yishmael before Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the threat of Yishmael is sharper now than ever, and answers that the Satan knows the fall of Yishmael ends the galus and his own power. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim on the end of Chayei Sarah and on the four pesukim with the word 'vekaras'.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah: Tziyon and the fear of Yishmael

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Rosh Hashanah tefillos and kriah ask for Moshiach: Sarah's remembrance hints at Tziyon, the seventh barren mother, and Sarah's banishing of Yishmael is the tefillah to be freed from the fear of Yishmael. He says a Jew should fear only Hashem, recalls the Scud attacks, and closes with brachos.

catalogTitle: ביטול כח עמלק שבזמן הזה; הסבר יסודות האמונה וביטול דיעות האפיקורסים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek's power is to explain everything as chance, and that the war against Amalek in Adar means seeing Hashem's hand in every event and knowing the foundations of emunah that no theory can shake.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy of Adar and the war against Amalek, whose essence is mikreh, chance: when all the chiefs of Edom trembled at the splitting of the sea, Amalek was not impressed. He recalls reading in Graetz's history that a freak wind split the sea, and brings the Ruzhiner's answer to a maskil that such a coincidence is an even greater miracle. The Megillah is a chain of such 'coincidences', and it teaches to see Hashem's hand in nature. He then explains why the Jewish emunah cannot be denied: an entire nation heard Hashem speak at Sinai, unlike religions founded on one individual, and he brings the Yismach Moshe on a mass event passed down from father to son. After explaining why one must speak about this today, he shows that evolution and the age-of-the-world theories are shifting speculation, and closes that the war against Amalek is knowing that every event comes from Hashem.

en: Amalek's essence is mikreh: he attributes everything to chance and denies hashgacha pratis.
Explaining the splitting of the sea as a coincidental wind is no more logical than a miracle; such a coincidence would itself be a greater miracle.
The Megillah is a chain of apparent coincidences, and it teaches to see Hashem's hand within nature.
Jewish emunah rests on what an entire nation saw and heard at Sinai, not on the claim of one individual.
An event witnessed by a multitude and passed on from father to son cannot be denied, just as no one denies Alexander the Great.
Evolution and the calculations of the world's age are shifting theories built on extrapolations that cannot be relied on.
The war against Amalek today is to know that every occurrence, in the world and in one's own life, comes from Hashem.

title.en: Adar, Amalek and chance

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy of Adar and the war against Amalek, whose essence is chance, as Haman called his downfall 'a coincidence'. He asks why Amalek, alone among the chiefs of Edom, was not shaken by the splitting of the sea.

title.en: Graetz's wind and the Ruzhiner's answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the apikorsus of the Yiddish papers in his youth and how he read in Graetz's history that a freak wind split the sea. He argues this is not more logical than a miracle, and brings the Ruzhiner's answer that such timing would be an even greater miracle.

title.en: The Megillah's chain of coincidences

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the Megillah as a series of 'just then' events, from Vashti to Charvonah, and explains that it teaches to see Hashem's hand in nature, which is the destruction of Amalek. Amalek's attack before Matan Torah cooled the acceptance of the Torah until it was accepted anew in the days of Achashverosh.

title.en: An entire nation heard Hashem speak

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Jewish emunah cannot be denied because six hundred thousand men with their families heard Hashem at Sinai, unlike Christianity, founded on one individual. He adds that milah is kept because of the command at Sinai, and that the people believe in Moshe Rabbeinu because they heard Hashem appoint him.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe on a mass event

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yismach Moshe's answer to someone troubled by doubts in emunah: not to philosophize, but to rely on what a whole multitude saw, which cannot be denied, as no one denies Alexander the Great. The Torah was seen by millions, written and handed down from father to son, and even the other religions admit it, only claiming that Hashem changed His mind, which cannot be.

title.en: Why these matters must be spoken of today

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he never spoke of these matters publicly, since it was not the custom, but today everyone comes into contact with these ideas, and the Skverer Rebbe says one must speak to children and bachurim. He mentions a doctor who began explaining evolution to him when he came for medical advice.

title.en: The folly of a world that made itself

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the claim that the world came about by itself to saying that a wise, beautifully written sefer was splashed onto its pages by a wind blowing over a bottle of ink, or that a computer evolved by itself. He notes that universities teach evolution only as a theory and that the more science learns, the less sense the theories make.

title.en: Scientific theories keep changing

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how theories change: the sun was held to circle the earth, Copernicus reversed it, and with Einstein's relativity both views are equally valid. He explains that scientists are driven by the wish for new discoveries and fame, and that belief in the Creator would bind them to the mitzvos, so their claims about billions of years are speculation.

title.en: Why their dating cannot be trusted

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains how a thermometer is built on a measured rate of expansion, and how water surprises by expanding again as it freezes, so no rate can be extrapolated back over a billion years. The same holds for the salt in the sea, rock layers and dinosaur bones: other conditions of pressure and temperature may have existed, and their proofs contradict each other.

title.en: The Mabul and the harmony of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the boiling waters of the Mabul, covering even the highest mountains, could bring about in a short time changes they calculate as taking a billion years, like a potato that softens in minutes when cooked. He then points to the harmony of creation and compares the unseen life in a creature to electricity in a wire, known by its effects.

title.en: The war against Amalek today

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Amalek, who called even the splitting of the sea a coincidence, and says today's devices bring Amalek's influence into the home. The war against Amalek is to know that every event is from Hashem, as the Megillah teaches and as the Ramban writes, and he closes with brachos for the coming year and for the geulah.

catalogTitle: יכולים למצוא השי"ת בחודש אדר ובכל מאורעות הזמן

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar is the 'heel' of time, a month of garments and hiddenness, and that its avodah is to find Hashem's name hidden in the events of the world, as in the Megillah, and to laugh at the costumes of history.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the Tanya's question: if every Jewish soul is truly G-dly, how can Moshe Rabbeinu's generation be the 'head' and the final generations the 'heels'? He answers that the inner point is the same in all; only the garments differ. Since soul, time and place parallel each other, time too has a head, Nisan, the month of open miracles, and heels, Adar, the month of garments. The last generations, like the Torah's last parshiyos, live in hester within hester. The avodah of Adar is to find Hashem's name in the 'megillah' of world events, to know that 'the King' is Hashem, and to laugh at the costumes. He develops this through Yaakov's descent to Egypt, Mordechai and David sparing Shimi, rulers as puppets, the Maharal on the speed of the Purim miracle and Naftali's swiftness, ending with simcha within hester.

en: All Jewish souls are truly G-dly; the difference between the great early generations and the last ones lies only in how many garments cover the same inner point.
Like the soul, time has a head and heels: Nisan, the month of revealed miracles, is the head, and Adar, the furthest point from Nisan, is the heels, a month of garments.
The avodah of Adar is to search for Hashem's name in the world's events, in the news and in one's own experiences, just as the mekubalim found His name hidden in the Megillah.
One who knows that 'the King' means Hashem is not frightened by the costumes of history but laughs at them, and laughter is the trait of Adar.
The rulers of the world are like puppets moved by strings from above; what matters is not who sits in power but the King, Hashem.
Events that happen with great speed are a sign of Hashem's hand, as the Maharal says of the Purim miracle, and Adar, the month of Naftali, is a swift month.
The joy of Purim comes not from what one has but from seeing Hashem's name, so one can be b'simcha even within hester.

candidateTopics: Mordechai and the decree of Haman

title.en: The generations as one body: head and heels

summary.en: After brief opening words, the Mashgiach describes the generations as one body, with Moshe Rabbeinu's generation the head and the generations before Moshiach the heels. He raises the Tanya's question of how souls that are truly G-dly can differ in level, and reads its answer of the son drawn from the father's mind.

title.en: Same inner point, different garments

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the inner point of every Jew is the same in the head as in the heels; the difference is only how much physicality covers it. Like a fetus that needs nine months to form, Moshe Rabbeinu's soul came with few garments and the souls before Moshiach with many.

title.en: Nisan the head of time, Adar its heels

summary.en: Since place, time and soul parallel each other, the Mashgiach shows that time too has a head, Nisan, 'rosh chodashim', and heels, Adar, the month furthest from Nisan. Nisan, from 'nes', is a month of open miracles, while Adar, from 'aderes', a cloak, is wrapped in garments.

title.en: The last generations and the Torah's last parshiyos

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the souls of the heels to the Torah's order: Bereishis corresponds to Moshe Rabbeinu, and today's souls to the last parshiyos, where there is no one to ask and Hashem says He will hide His face. In the heels there is a hester within hester, which the Ba'al Shem Tov spoke of.

title.en: Adar, Adar Sheini and Megillas Esther

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Adar a month of garments in which Hashem appears hidden. When the hester seems to end, a second Adar begins, hester upon hester. He brings the Kozhnitzer Maggid on the name 'Megillas Esther' and notes that Jews make a brachah on the miracles of a Megillah that seems to tell only ordinary events and never names Hashem.

title.en: Costumes, 'the King', and the hidden Name

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all the events of the Megillah are miracles clothed in nature, and that the custom of dressing up teaches that garments mean nothing: Chazal say 'the King' in the Megillah means Hashem. From Purim one leaves knowing that the hidden guidance is also His, and the mekubalim found His name in the Megillah's roshei teivos at its turning points.

title.en: Searching for Hashem in the world, and laughing

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the avodah of Adar is to find Hashem's name in the 'megillah' of the world, where He peers through the cracks. A child is frightened by a man dressed as Haman, but one who sees Hashem's name laughs. Adar's organ is the spleen, the source of laughter, so its avodah is to laugh at the newspapers and commentators and to know that 'the King' is Hashem.

title.en: The claim against Europe's rabbis, and Yaakov's descent to Egypt

summary.en: The Mashgiach takes up the claim that the rabbis and rebbes of Europe erred by not urging Jews toward Eretz Yisrael before the war. He answers from Yaakov Avinu: his going down to Egypt could look like a mistake, but it was a decree from Hashem, and Chazal say he would otherwise have been brought in iron chains. Instead of complaining 'my way is hidden', one should look through the cracks of the hester.

title.en: Achashverosh's feast and the complaints against Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Megillah's story unfolding over years. Mordechai cried out not to go to Achashverosh's feast, though everything there was kosher, yet many Jews went; later he refused to bow to Haman, and Jews blamed him for the decree.

title.en: Ish Yehudi and Ish Yemini: David and Shimi

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks who really caused the decree and brings the Gemara on 'ish Yehudi … ish Yemini': Knesses Yisrael complains that David did not kill Shimi, from whom Mordechai descended. At the end of the Megillah it became clear that David's mercy was the cause of the rescue, because David saw Hashem's name even in Shimi's curse, and measure for measure he brought forth Mordechai, who revealed the hester.

title.en: Rulers as puppets and the 'Jewish question'

summary.en: The Mashgiach says rulers are marionettes on strings from above, so it makes no difference who sits in the White House; it depends on the King. He notes that the whole world revolves around the Jews, that a progressive nation followed a leader set on 'solving the Jewish question', and tells of an old Jew angered at having to wait six hours after meat, explaining that the very existence of Jews proclaims morality and arouses hatred.

title.en: Hiding until the wrath passes; the Maharal on speed

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the answer to the 'Jewish question' is 'chavi kim'at rega': go into your rooms, take your Gemara and Mishnayos and hide until the wrath passes, as Esther hid her origins. He then asks where the miracles of the Megillah are and brings the Maharal that they lie in the speed of the events, a sign of Hashem's hand, which he sees in his own times too.

title.en: Naftali, the swift tribe of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach links Adar to the tribe of Naftali, whom Yaakov blessed as 'ayalah sheluchah', not for a particular quality but for swiftness, and brings Chazal's account of Naftali running to bring the deed. When Jews are low and Amalek high, things happen with Naftali's speed, and so even amid distress one must learn to laugh and be b'simcha.

title.en: Simcha within hester, and Adar leading to Nisan

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against losing hope when the redemption seems delayed, and says the joy of Purim comes from seeing Hashem's name, so it can exist even within hester; in simcha alone one may go to extremes. He closes by joining Adar to Nisan, 'to join redemption to redemption'.

catalogTitle: וטוב לב משתה תמיד - להודות לה' ולהתקרב אליו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the halachic standing of the Purim Katan seudah according to the Rema and the Acharonim, and shows how 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid' means thanking Hashem and drawing close to Him even in a time of hiddenness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rema on Purim Katan: some say there is an obligation of mishteh v'simcha in Adar Rishon, the custom is otherwise, yet one should add a little to the meal, and 'a good heart is a constant feast.' He sets out the dispute behind it, with Tosfos holding that mishteh v'simcha belongs only to Adar Sheni, and brings the Magen Avraham and the Chasam Sofer that a place or family saved by a miracle may make a day of thanks. He concludes that the Purim Katan seudah is a mitzvah, not a chiyuv, may be held at night, and lacks the halachos of seudas Purim. He then explains the leap month as the moon, Knesses Yisroel, catching up to the sun, and teaches that thanking Hashem in hester panim gives Him great nachas, and that Adar is a time for tefillah.

en: The Rema rules that although the custom is not to treat Adar Rishon as a day of mishteh v'simcha, one should add somewhat to the meal on Purim Katan, ending with 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid'.

According to the Magen Avraham and the Chasam Sofer, a community or family that experienced a miracle may set a day of celebration, and the Mashgiach argues that Purim Katan should be no less than such a private Purim.
The Mashgiach concludes that the Purim Katan seudah is a mitzvah but not an obligation, may be held at night, and does not require the halachos of seudas Purim.
The leap month exists so that the lunar year can catch up with the solar year, which the Mashgiach reads as Knesses Yisroel, the moon, returning to Hashem, the sun.
When Jews sit down to thank Hashem in a time of hester panim, without being commanded, it brings Him great nachas, and Adar is a time to pour out one's heart in tefillah.

candidateTopics: Adar as a time for tefillah

title.en: The Rema's ruling and the custom

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rema's words on Purim Katan, that some say there is an obligation of mishteh v'simcha but the custom is otherwise, and stresses that one does not rule against an established minhag.

title.en: A day of thanks for a private miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Magen Avraham and the Chasam Sofer that a community or family saved by a miracle may make a yearly day of celebration, sets out the dispute of the Rishonim on the Mishnah about Adar Rishon, and asks why Purim should be less than such a private day, since we are the descendants of those saved.

title.en: Tosfos and the nature of the seudah

summary.en: Following Tosfos, mishteh v'simcha as Mordechai's enactment belongs only to Adar Sheni and requires wine; the Mashgiach explains that a seudah in Adar Rishon would instead be thanks for the miracle, without all the laws of seudas Purim, and mentions Rabbi Avraham of Ciechanow drinking wine to fulfil the mitzvah.

title.en: Why the Rema says 'a little more in the meal'

summary.en: The Mashgiach analyzes the Rema's change of wording from 'mishteh v'simcha' to 'adding a little to the meal', showing that it follows the Magen Avraham's reasoning and does not uproot the custom, and explains 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid' as a meal with a glass of wine and l'chaim.

title.en: A seudah at night, on the day of the miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks whether a seudah that is a remembrance of the miracle may be held at night, and answers that it may; he discusses that such a remembrance belongs on the day the miracle happened, and suggests that this is the source of the custom to make a small seudah on the night of Purim Katan.

title.en: The leap month: the moon returns to the sun

summary.en: Bringing the tzaddikim that Adar Rishon is a month of teshuvah, the Mashgiach explains the leap month as the lunar year catching up with the solar year: the sun is Hashem, the moon is Knesses Yisroel, which drifted away through sin; Purim Katan is linked to the 'small luminary', and its feast is the joy of Knesses Yisroel returning to Hashem.

title.en: The last month repairs the year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last, added month can repair what was missed in the earlier months, brings the Midrash comparing Esther to the morning star at the end of the night, and describes the renewal it brings: a fresh acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, like a new creation.

title.en: An episode from the British Mandate

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of an episode in Eretz Yisroel under the British Mandate, connected to a planned public desecration of Shabbos.

title.en: L'chaim, and Haman's reckoning of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for l'chaim with wishes for health and the coming redemption, then turns to Haman, a master of calculations of times and lots, who rejoiced that his lot fell in Adar, the month of Moshe's passing, and connects his error to the intercalation of the year.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Seizing every chance to thank Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that some held the seudah should be by day, then teaches that a Jew should seize even the smallest occasion to thank Hashem, who is the same as for all earlier generations, and brings the Midrash that 'we will rejoice in Him' means rejoicing with Hashem rather than with the day.

title.en: The force of minhag and private Purims

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that a minhag decides even in weighty matters, then discusses private Purims set by communities in Europe saved from decrees, which the Chasam Sofer discusses, and the possibility that the Men of the Great Assembly enacted mishteh v'simcha only for Adar Sheni.

title.en: No less than the Purim of Amsterdam

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Purim Katan should be less than the private Purims of Cracow or Amsterdam, and concludes that making it a day of mishteh v'simcha is a mitzvah though not an obligation, so its seudah does not need the halachos of seudas Purim, like the joy of eating meat in the time of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: A gathering with l'chaim and blessings

summary.en: Returning to the Rema's wording, the Mashgiach describes the custom: Jews sit together at a private gathering, sing, pour a glass of wine, say l'chaim and bless one another, which he calls 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid'; it may be at night or whenever one wishes, since no halachos bind it.

title.en: Rejoicing in Hashem, not in the day

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the Midrash adds by reading 'nagilah v'nismecha bo' as rejoicing with Hashem, and explains that one can rejoice with Hashem even when the time does not call for it; he then describes the descent through the generations to the lowest time, when Knesses Yisroel, the moon, is far from the sun in exile.

title.en: From 'shivisi' to 'tov lev mishteh tamid'

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the halachos of Purim Katan are the last in Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim, which opens with 'shivisi Hashem l'negdi tamid' and closes with 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid'; in the twelfth month, in the darkness of hester panim when no salvation comes, Jews still make a seudah to thank Hashem, with emunah in the nights.

title.en: Uncommanded thanks and tefillah in Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that when Jews in hester panim sit down to thank Hashem without being commanded, Purim Katan can accomplish more than Purim itself, connecting this to 'yehei shmei rabba' and to Esther pleading before the king. He closes by calling Adar a time to pour out one's heart in tefillah for the geulah of Nissan.

catalogTitle: “אנה לידו ושמתי לך מקום” - The Essence of the מצוה of ערי מקלט: Seek Hashem as your Refuge.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Elul is an ir miklat, a city of refuge from the Satan, and that the true refuge in place, time, Torah and soul is always Malchus Shamayim, which Moshiach, whose own mitzvah is the cities of refuge, will complete.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the remez that Elul is a city of refuge, from the passuk 'ina l'yado v'samti lecha makom', and identifies the pursuing avenger with the Satan and the yetzer hara. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that the Satan will err by fleeing to Bozrah instead of Betzer, and asks how such a lamdan could err so plainly. Through the Rambam's three Torah sources for Moshiach, he shows that the unfulfilled mitzvah of adding three cities waits for Moshiach, and proposes that this is Moshiach's own mitzvah. Using the Sefer Yetzirah's place, time and soul, he finds a refuge in each, plus Kriyas Shema in the Torah, all of them Malchus Shamayim. The Satan panics in Betzer because he senses Moshiach there, and flees to Bozrah, the source of Moav's malchus of tumah. The Mashgiach urges running to Torah and teshuvah rather than the protections of the nations, and ends with the 122 days of teshuvah hinted in the sedras.

en: Elul is an ir miklat, hinted in the passuk 'ina l'yado v'samti lecha', and the avenger it protects from is the Satan, the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death.
The Gemara in Makkos says the Satan will err and flee to Bozrah, thinking it is a city of refuge, though the Torah names Betzer.
The mitzvah of adding three more cities of refuge was never fulfilled and waits for Moshiach; the Mashgiach proposes that it is Moshiach's own mitzvah, through which he completes the Torah.
There is a city of refuge in place, in time (Elul through Yom Kippur), in the Torah (Kriyas Shema) and in the soul (Moshiach), and all of them are Malchus Shamayim.
In a time of fear, the Mashgiach says, Jews should run to Torah, mitzvos, teshuvah, bitachon and emunah, and not to the protections of the nations, which are Bozrah.
The teshuvah season stretches from Elul as far as Chanukah, and the 122 pesukim of Ki Savo are a rebuke for last year's unused 122 days.

candidateTopics: Moshiach and the mitzvah of ir miklat

title.en: Elul as a city of refuge

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Elul already begins and shapes the new year, brings the remez of 'Ani l'dodi', and then the remez of 'ina l'yado v'samti lecha', which makes Elul an ir miklat. The avenger who pursues a person is the Satan, the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death.

title.en: Yaakov's flight to Sukkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that the sequence of Elul, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos is found in Yaakov's encounter with Esav: the brachos, the gift to Esav's angel, and finally the flight to Sukkos, where he is sheltered by the Shechinah. On Sukkos Jews take refuge under the wings of the Shechinah like a child under its mother's apron.

title.en: The Satan's mistake: Bozrah, not Betzer

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Makkos that at the Geulah the Satan will flee to Bozrah, erring three ways. He focuses on the error of Bozrah: the Satan is a great lamdan who can dress an aveirah as a mitzvah, and every child knows the passuk says Betzer, so why does he run to Bozrah?

title.en: The Rambam: three places that promise Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that three places in the Torah promise Moshiach, the third being the mitzvah to add three cities of refuge, which was never fulfilled. He then lists the Rambam's three simanim of Moshiach, matches them to the three places, and explains through arvus that the whole of Klal Yisrael has fulfilled every mitzvah except this one, which waits for Moshiach.

title.en: Moshiach's own mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the 600,000 root souls correspond to the letters of the Sefer Torah and that every Jew is rooted in one particular mitzvah, as in the Gemara 'with which mitzvah was your father most careful'. He asks what Moshiach's own mitzvah is, and proposes that it is ir miklat, since through it he completes the Torah and is the savior who is Klal Yisrael's refuge.

title.en: A refuge in place, time, Torah and soul

summary.en: From the Sefer Yetzirah's olam, shanah, nefesh, the Mashgiach shows that the ir miklat exists in place (the cities), in Torah (the 6 and 42 words of Shema matching the 48 cities), in time (Elul through Yom Kippur) and in the soul (Moshiach). All of them are kabbalas ol Malchus Shamayim, and he brings the Tzemach Tzedek that a king, and above all Melech HaMashiach, is wholly nullified to Hashem.

title.en: Moshe begins, Moshiach completes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the king's fear of Heaven spreads to the people, that Moshe was the first king and first redeemer and Moshiach the last, sharing one soul. Moshe designated the first cities of refuge and Moshiach will add the last three; he shows by gematria that both phrases equal 'som tasim alecha melech'.

title.en: Why the Satan flees Betzer for Bozrah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the shofar confuses the Satan because it reminds him of the shofar of Moshiach. Returning to the opening question, he explains that in Betzer the Satan senses Moshiach, for Betzer in the Zohar's ribua gematria equals David ben Yishai, panics, and argues that Bozrah is Betzer's feminine form, since in tumah the feminine dominates, as the Ohr HaChaim describes. But Bozrah is exactly where Hashem will slaughter the Satan.

title.en: Moav exports malchus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shem MiShmuel quoting his father-in-law, the Kotzker, that malchus is foreign to Yisrael and was imported from Moav through Rus. Rashi explains that Bozrah, a city of Moav, gave Edom its king, Yovav ben Zerach, so the Satan flees from the malchus of kedushah in Betzer to the malchus of tumah in Bozrah, which Moshiach will destroy.

title.en: Run to Torah, not to Bozrah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the fear in the world and in Eretz Yisrael today, and says those who lack emunah run to Bozrah. He brings the Gemara in Makkos that the Torah is a city of refuge, and recalls how gedolim, among them Rav Chaim Kanievsky, kept learning during the missile attacks instead of running to sealed rooms; the true refuge is Torah, mitzvos, teshuvah and emunah.

title.en: 30, 40, 52 and 122 days of teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tzaddikim need only the 30 days of Elul, beinonim need 40, and that the Zohar and the Arizal extend teshuvah to Shemini Atzeres and even the last day of Chanukah. He shows that the sedras read now have matching numbers of pesukim: Vayelech 30, Nitzavim 40, Haazinu 52, and together 122, the days until Chanukah, and notes his son-in-law's remark that Ki Savo also has 122.

title.en: Ki Savo: last year's 122 days

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Ki Savo's 122 pesukim, read so the year ends with its curses, point to last year's 122 days of teshuvah and the tragedies that followed, as a rebuke not to repeat the mistake. He calls on everyone to use Elul and Tishrei, run to the refuge under the Shechinah's apron, and closes with brachos for a good year and the coming of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: האור של מגילת אסתר יותר נעלה מאור של תורת משה (חתם סופר)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Megillah has two faces, the level of Kesuvim all year and on Purim a light higher even than Toras Moshe, and that through it Klal Yisroel, even in its lowest state, is revealed as Hashem's kallah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a Megillah written among the other books of Kesuvim is not valid, and with Esther's place among the prophetesses. He explains that certain parts of Torah have two faces: the Aseres HaDibros read with the upper or lower cantillation, and the song of David in Navi and in Tehillim. So too the Megillah: all year it is Kesuvim, but on Purim a higher world comes down and, as the Chasam Sofer writes, its light is greater than that of Toras Moshe. For this Esther had to be a prophetess. He then explains that Purim is for those who have fallen far: 'lechalosam' in the days of Haman means 'to His kallah', like a king who goes to his bride in a disgraceful place. 'Al mikra megillah' equals 'chosson v'kallah'. He applies this to Purim Katan, to the small avodah of today, and ends with joy and brachos for the chosson and kallah.

en: A Megillah written among the other books of Kesuvim is not valid, because on Purim the Megillah rises above the level of Kesuvim.
Some parts of Torah have two faces, a higher and a lower level, such as the Aseres HaDibros with the upper and lower cantillation.
Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach says the greatness of the Megillah on Purim is higher than the light of Toras Moshe.
Purim belongs to the Jews who have fallen far; even there they remain Hashem's kallah.
The words 'al mikra megillah' in the bracha equal 'chosson v'kallah' in gematria.

title.en: A Megillah among the Kesuvim; Esther the prophetess

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a Megillah written among the other books of Kesuvim is not valid, and asks how this fits the bracha 'al mikra megillah'. He brings the Gemara's count of prophets and prophetesses, Rashi on why Daniel is not counted, and Esther's place among the prophetesses, and mentions how Haman's decree bound all Jews together.

title.en: Two faces in Torah; the Chasam Sofer on the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Aseres HaDibros read in public with the upper cantillation are on a higher level than when read alone, and that the song of David stands higher in Navi than in Tehillim. He brings the Yerushalmi that the Megillah will remain when other books are annulled, and the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah's greatness is higher than the light of Toras Moshe.

title.en: The Megillah's new light on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Megillah is Kesuvim all year but on Purim receives a new light, which is why one written among the Kesuvim is invalid. To write it above the Kesuvim, Esther had to be a prophetess; he connects 'vatilbash Esther malchus' and the inner court of the king to the world where all Jews are bound together at the root of their souls.

title.en: Purim for the fallen; 'lechalosam' as His kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Purim is for those who have fallen far, and that the hidden love of Hashem, which many waters cannot extinguish, is revealed through the Megillah. He reads the Gemara's 'lechalosam' in the days of Haman as 'to His kallah', with a mashal of a king who goes to his bride in a disgraceful place to bring her back.

title.en: Esther cries out; 'al mikra megillah' as chosson v'kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Esther crying out to Hashem from the lowest place, and says the joy of Purim is that Jews know that in whatever state they are, even outside the camp, they are Hashem's kallah. Therefore the bracha 'al mikra megillah' equals 'chosson v'kallah' in gematria.

title.en: Purim Katan and the heavenly yeshiva

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that although the Megillah is read in the second Adar, the joy belongs to Purim Katan too, and that in Heaven there is a yeshiva that follows Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Yosi, where the Megillah is read today. He adds that on Purim a Jew may enter the heichal of whichever tanna he wishes, and that a small avodah of today, such as negel vasser, is precious in Heaven.

title.en: Joy of chosson and kallah; brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Jews gather to strengthen the emunah that they are Hashem's kallah, connects 'vaye'ehav hamelech es Esther' to the joy of chosson and kallah, and blesses the chosson, kallah and families. He closes with 'tov lev mishteh tamid' and the hope that the joy may help bring Moshiach.
